item.title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation
item.description: By Koutian Wu, Junjie Zhou, Ergan Shang (Hangzhou Dianzi University; Carnegie Mellon University; Xi'an Jiaotong University; The University of Auckland; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Tsinghua University) Good evening, and welcome back to Papercast. We open tonight with Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation, from Koutian Wu, Junjie Zhou, and Ergan Shang, working across Hangzhou Dianzi University, Carnegie Mellon University, and Xi'an Jiaotong University. This is not a model and it is not a new training method. It is infrastructure, a maintained database plus a search engine over AI benchmarks, and the honest question it is trying to answer is whether anyone can actually keep a trustworthy map of what every model claims to be good at. Here is the problem, stated plainly. Evaluation in this field is fragmented across at least three well known surfaces. LLM Stats publishes benchmark names with descriptions and source provenance. OpenCompass Hub carries paper, repository, release, and dataset links. Artificial Analysis runs a catalog of current commercial evaluation entries. Each one is real, each one is partial, and none of them agrees on what a "benchmark" even is. So a researcher who wants to compare two models on, say, a long-horizon terminal task has to hunt across sites, reconcile scores that were measured under different settings, and guess whether a number on one leaderboard is even comparable to a number on another. The paper's premise is that this reconciliation work should live in one auditable place, updated on a schedule, rather than being redone by hand every time someone writes a model report.

item.title: Breaking the Vision-Action Shortcut: Latent Interface Training for Generalizable Robotics Foundation Models
item.description: By Jianman Lin, Shailesh Shailesh, Zhongyi Luo (National University of Singapore; Nanyang Technological University) Good evening, we are back, and tonight's second paper is Breaking the Vision-Action Shortcut: Latent Interface Training for Generalizable Robotics Foundation Models, from Jianman Lin, Shailesh Shailesh, and Zhongyi Luo, with the first two at the National University of Singapore and Zhongyi Luo at Nanyang Technological University. This is a robotics foundation model paper, specifically a vision-language-action model, and it attacks a failure mode that is much more common than people admit: the model learns to copy the visual correlation it saw in the demonstrations instead of learning the actual task geometry, and then it falls apart the moment the camera, the lighting, or the objects on the table change. Let me name the problem precisely, because the whole method hangs on it. A robot foundation model that generates actions from pretrained visual representations achieves strong in-distribution performance, but under visual distribution shift it degrades. The reason, as the paper frames it, is that the model exploits task-irrelevant visual cues that merely correlate with the demonstrated actions within the training distribution. They call these vision-action shortcuts. The image is doing double duty in these models. It is carrying the semantic instruction, the robot state, and also a lot of incidental background that happened to be present in every demonstration. When you change the camera position or the lighting, that incidental structure changes, and the shortcut that was a reliable predictor in training becomes an unreliable one at test time. The goal is to constrain how visual information is used for action generation, while still preserving the task-relevant spatial information you actually need.

item.title: SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking
item.description: By Zhiwei Li, Lei Zhu, Hao Gu (Tencent HY LLM Frontier; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) Good evening, paper three tonight is SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking, from Zhiwei Li, Lei Zhu, and Hao Gu, working out of the Tencent HY LLM Frontier team and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Guangzhou. This one falls squarely into the reasoning-model topology bucket, because it changes the attention computation itself. The pitch is that you can sparsify a long-context transformer's attention, cut the number of keys and values each query has to attend to, and do it end-to-end by learning a context ranking, and that doing it the simple way is enough to beat a lot of the more elaborate sparse-attention schemes. The motivation is the standard long-context cost problem, so I will be brief. Full attention is quadratic in sequence length. For long contexts, that is where both the time and the memory go. Sparse attention methods attack this by making each query attend to only a subset of the keys and values, and the hard part is deciding which subset. You need a way to rank the context by relevance, and you need that ranking to actually track what the full attention would have weighted, or your accuracy dies. Most prior methods use a hand-designed or heuristic rule for the selection. A sliding window, a fixed stride, or a separate learned selector trained with its own surrogate loss. The problem with a separate selector trained on a surrogate is a mismatch. The selector optimizes an approximation of the objective, while the downstream transformer is optimizing the real one, and the two do not always agree.

item.title: COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization
item.description: By Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, Xiang Li (The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen; Tianjin University; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); National University of Singapore) Good evening, back again, and tonight's fourth paper is COBRA-Skills: Contextual Bandit-Guided Evolution for Agent Skill Optimization, from Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang, and Xiang Li, at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Tianjin University, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Guangzhou. This is an agent-efficiency paper, and the problem it tackles is a real cost problem anyone running LLM agents knows. If you want to teach your agent reusable skills, distilled from prior task experience, the standard approach is an execution-based loop. You generate candidate skills, you run the agent on tasks to see which ones actually help, and you refine. The catch is that running the agent is the expensive part, and most of the budget can get burned evaluating skills that were never going to be any good. Let me frame the gap precisely. Reusable skills are a lightweight way to capture procedural knowledge. A skill is a chunk of task-specific guidance, a reasoning strategy, or a tool-use procedure, that you inject into the agent's context when it solves a new instance. Manually writing good skills is slow and requires domain expertise. Generating them directly from the model's parametric knowledge produces plausible-sounding but ungrounded guidance that does not reliably help. So recent work grounds skill construction in actual trajectories and execution feedback, and several methods add iterative evolutionary refinement, generating, revising, and selecting stronger skills from accumulated experience. item.title: PLC-DPO: Posterior Label Correction in Noisy and Ambiguous Preference Optimization
item.description: By Boryeong Cho, Sumyeong Ahn, Se-Young Yun (KAIST AI; KENTECH) Good evening, paper five tonight is PLC-DPO: Posterior Label Correction in Noisy and Ambiguous Preference Optimization, from Boryeong Cho, Sumyeong Ahn, and Se-Young Yun, working at KAIST AI and KENTECH. This is an alignment objective paper, and it is one of those that starts from a flaw that is almost universal in preference optimization. Direct Preference Optimization, DPO, is now the standard offline alignment objective. It is simple, it is scalable, it sidesteps training a separate reward model, and it fits a Bradley-Terry preference model directly from the policy-reference log-ratio. But the whole thing rests on an assumption that real data violates constantly. It assumes every observed preference, every chosen over rejected pair, is a reliable target. Here is the problem, stated plainly. In reality, preference labels suffer from annotator disagreement, model-judge biases, and superficial cues like length or confident wording. And true preferences are not always strictly directional in the first place. Two responses might be equally good, equally bad, or so marginally different that they do not support a stable binary signal. When DPO treats every label as absolute ground truth, it actively reinforces the wrong optimization direction whenever a pair is flipped or weak. That is the gap this paper targets, and it is a real gap, not a toy one.

item.title: Feyospace-v1: How the Cyber Mercury Seven Trained Frontier Cyber Models
item.description: By The Feyospace Team (Feyospace) Good evening, and our final paper tonight is Feyospace-v1: How the Cyber Mercury Seven Trained Frontier Cyber Models, from the Feyospace team. This is a training-report paper, and I want to be straight with you up front about how I am reading it. The title has a certain swagger to it, the Cyber Mercury Seven, and the team is not naming individual authors in the way a normal paper would. That anonymity is itself a data point, and I will come back to it. What the paper is actually about, stripped of the branding, is a data pipeline and a post-training recipe for open-weight cyber and security reasoning models. Let me tell you what it does, because the substance is where the interesting and the questionable both live. The setting is security task reasoning. The target capabilities are the ones that matter in real offensive and defensive security work. Vulnerability discovery, exploit development, CTF-style challenge solving, patch generation, and reasoning over real codebases. The team's core claim is that they built a pipeline that turns a large corpus of real-world security tasks into executable, verifiable training environments, and that post-training open-weight checkpoints on those environments produces models that are competitive on security benchmarks. The three checkpoints they train are Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B, and a third open-weight base. So this is not a new foundation model. It is a post-training, supervised fine-tuning effort on top of existing open-weight bases, and I am flagging that because it shapes how much weight the results carry.

item.title: NCP-ArchPreview Technical Report: Moving Towards Latent Space Language Models through Next Concept Prediction
item.description: By The Intern-NCP Team (Jiaqi Cao, Chiyu Chen, Shuang Cheng, et al.) (Shanghai AI Lab; LUMIA Lab, Shanghai Jiao Tong University) Good evening, and welcome back to Papercast. I'm your host, and tonight we start with a paper that I think deserves the top spot for good reason: NCP-ArchPreview, a technical report from the Intern-NCP Team at Shanghai AI Lab and the LUMIA Lab at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. This is a report on what they call a latent-space language model, and it is built on top of one of the most respected open model families we cover on this show, OLMo. If you follow the open-model scene, you already know that OLMo has been one of the most methodical open pretraining efforts out there, and this is a genuinely architectural experiment layered on top of it, not just a new training recipe. So what is the core idea? Every modern language model you have ever used, including the one reading these words, is trained to do one thing: predict the next token. One word, or one fragment of a word, at a time. That next-token prediction objective is so deeply baked into the field that most of us treat it as the only way to train a language model. NCP-ArchPreview says, what if we add a second, harder objective on top of it? Not just predict the next token, but also predict the next concept, where a concept is a discrete unit of meaning that spans multiple tokens. Here is how that works in practice. item.title: SenseNova-U1.5: Towards Native Unified Visual Intelligence
item.description: By Haiwen Diao, Jiahao Wang, Chenjing Ding (SenseNova) Good evening, welcome back to Papercast. I'm your host, and tonight's second paper is SenseNova U1.5, from the SenseNova team, with Haiwen Diao, Jiahao Wang, and Chenjing Ding among the authors, and this is a large industrial team effort. This is a foundation-model release, which is why it is on this show even though it came in second in the upvote race: the standing rule is that any paper introducing a new foundation model gets an episode, and SenseNova U1.5 is unambiguously that. It is the next generation of what the SenseNova team calls a natively unified model, one that understands and generates images inside a single network rather than bolting a separate image generator on. Let me set the stage with the problem. For most of the last few years, the standard recipe for a multimodal model has been modular. You take a large language model. You attach a vision encoder, a separate neural network whose only job is to turn pixels into vectors. You train an adapter, or a projector, to translate those visual vectors into the language model's space. Understanding works well with this design. But if you want the model to generate images, the modular design falls apart, because the vision encoder is a one-way street: it can read images, but it cannot write them. So every lab that wants both capabilities has to bolt on a second system, usually a diffusion model or an autoregressive image tokenizer, and manage the handoff between the two.

item.title: EvoSafeHarness: Evolving Model- and Domain-Specific Harnesses for Securing Agents
item.description: By Nanxi Li, Yingzi Ma, Yulong Cao (Johns Hopkins University, NVIDIA, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, UC Berkeley) Good evening, welcome back to Papercast. I'm your host, and tonight's third paper is EvoSafeHarness, from Nanxi Li, Yingzi Ma, and Yulong Cao, with the team spanning Johns Hopkins University, NVIDIA, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and UC Berkeley. This is an agent safety paper, and it is a good example of where this subfield is heading: instead of patching the model, the authors build and evolve a custom safety harness around it. The harness is the wrapper system, the policies and the code that sits between the user's request and the model's actions. The problem, in one sentence: large language model agents are increasingly given access to real tools, emails, files, browsers, and accounts, and that access makes them exposed to two kinds of threats. The first is indirect prompt injection, where a malicious instruction is hidden inside some document or webpage the agent is supposed to read, and the agent obeys it as if the user had asked. The second is direct harmful requests, where the user themselves asks the agent to do something unsafe. The standard response to both is to add guardrails, but most guardrails are generic, hand-written rules that either block too much and hurt the agent's usefulness, or are tuned to one specific benchmark and fail when the deployment changes. There is also a practical asymmetry that the paper leans on: the model's weights are often frozen at deployment time. The organization running the agent usually did not train the model, and retraining a frontier model to be safer is not an option available to them. That means the practical place to put safety work is the wrapper, and that is exactly where EvoSafeHarness lives.

item.title: SpatialBlock: Enhancing Spatial Intelligence in LVLMs via Synthetic Block-Stacking Problem
item.description: By Soohyun Ryu, Sohee Kim, Eunho Yang (KAIST) Good evening, welcome back to Papercast. I'm your host, and tonight's fourth paper is SpatialBlock, from Soohyun Ryu, Sohee Kim, and Eunho Yang at KAIST in South Korea. This is a spatial reasoning paper for vision-language models, and it has one of the most honest framings I have seen all week: the authors start from the observation that state-of-the-art vision-language models are bad at something that most humans find easy, and then they build a small, synthetic training set to fix it. The setup is a demonstration of the gap. The paper leads with a simple block-stacking problem: you are shown a 3D structure made of blocks, and you are asked how it looks from a particular viewing direction, which is a mental rotation and projection task. Humans solve these at near-perfect rates, around 95 percent in their figure. GPT-5 gets about 30 percent. Qwen 2.5 7B gets about 21 percent. That is the motivation in a single chart: the leading models have flawed spatial logic, they cannot even reliably do the basic version of a task that developmental psychology has studied for decades. The key insight is borrowed from how humans actually learn spatial skills. Developmental psychology has shown that foundational spatial abilities are built through structured manipulative play, and block play specifically is one of the best-studied examples. So instead of the usual approach, which is to scrape real-world 3D scenes and label them with dense geometric annotations using external segmentation and depth models, an expensive and noisy process, the authors generate a synthetic dataset of block-stacking problems. The dataset is called SpatialBlock-15k, and it has 15,000 problems in three categories, each with 5,000 examples.

item.title: CARDEA: Auditable Reasoning Grounded in Spatial Evidence for End-to-End Coronary Angiography Interpretation
item.description: By Jia-Jen Lee, Shih-Yen Hou, Kee Koon Ng (China Medical University Hospital, China Medical University) Good evening, and welcome to the final paper of tonight's episode. I'm your host, and this one is CARDEA, from Jia-Jen Lee, Shih-Yen Hou, and Kee Koon Ng, a clinical and AI collaboration at China Medical University Hospital and China Medical University in Taichung, Taiwan. This is a medical imaging paper, and it is the kind of paper that tends to be easy to skim past and hard to overestimate, so I want to be careful about both. The system is a large vision-language model that runs an end-to-end pipeline for interpreting coronary angiography, and its distinguishing feature is that it shows its spatial work. The clinical context. Invasive coronary angiography, or CAG, is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease. A catheter is threaded to the heart, contrast is injected, and a series of X-ray videos of the coronary arteries is captured from multiple angles. The problem is that these are 2D projections of a 3D structure, so vessels overlap and foreshorten, and a clinician has to mentally integrate several views of each lesion to judge how bad a narrowing really is. This is genuinely hard, and it is not consistent even among experts: the paper cites a study where three experienced cardiologists reading the same angiograms had an overall agreement of about 77 percent. That means roughly a quarter of the time, two experienced specialists disagree.

item.title: Recursive Code World Models: Building Complex Worlds through Recursive Scene Programs
item.description: By Zhiqi Li, Yuxuan Liao, Bo Zhu (Georgia Institute of Technology) Good evening, welcome back to Papercast. I'm your host, and tonight's fifth paper is Recursive Code World Models, from Zhiqi Li, Yuxuan Liao, and Bo Zhu at the Georgia Institute of Technology. This is a 3D generation paper, and it comes out of a trend I have been covering a lot this year: the idea that a 3D world is better represented not as a cloud of points or a mesh, but as an executable program, a piece of code that, when you run it, renders the scene. Let me frame the problem. There is now a family of methods, sometimes called code world models, that take a single reference image and produce a 3D world expressed as code, typically in something like Three.js or Blender. The appeal of code is real: it is editable, you can reuse components, you can hand it to a physics simulator, and you can inspect the geometry directly rather than reverse-engineering it from rendered pixels. But there has always been a gap between the representation and the construction. Knowing that code is a good way to represent a world does not tell you how to actually build a complex one from a single image. That is the gap this paper addresses. The core idea is to make the construction process itself recursive. The authors define a representation they call a Recursive Scene Program, an RSP, which represents the executable world as compositional scene code, with parts that can call other parts. And they pair it with a construction solver that recursively calls itself. Every call to the solver follows the same complete process, no matter what scale you are at. item.title: Show-Harness: Just a VLM Agent Can Play Robots
item.description: By Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, Zhijun Cao (Show Lab, National University of Singapore) Show-Harness, presenting a way to let a single vision-language model drive a real robot without any fine-tuning. Lead contributors from Show Lab at the National University of Singapore, with Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, and Zhijun Cao as co-first authors. The core claim is that the bottleneck in robot manipulation is not the model's intelligence but the interface between the model's semantic world and the robot's physical actuators. If you design that interface right, a frontier VLM can pick up a banana and put it on a plate with zero training data. The problem they are attacking is a real tension in the field. Vision-language-action models, the dominant paradigm, fine-tune a VLM to regress continuous robot actions. That works, but it collapses the model's broad semantic knowledge into an opaque pixel-to-motor mapping. Every new robot arm, every new task family, every new environment requires fresh trajectories and retraining. Hierarchical systems go the other direction: the VLM emits subtasks or programs, but a separate controller handles the physical execution, which severs the direct link between what the model intends and what the robot actually does. Show-Harness sits in the middle. It defines a compact set of discrete semantic action units, things like move forward, move right, grasp, release, rotate clockwise. Each unit is one small, bounded motion. The VLM picks the unit; a deterministic embodiment-specific interpreter maps it to a concrete joint-space trajectory. The VLM stays responsible for fine-grained physical decisions, but it never has to predict a continuous action vector.

item.title: Programmable World Model
item.description: By Zheng-Hui Huang, Guixu Lin, Jiacheng Lin (Alaya Lab) Programmable World Model, from Alaya Lab, with Zheng-Hui Huang, Guixu Lin, and Jiacheng Lin as the leading authors. The pitch is that video world models can generate convincing interactive scenes but have no idea what is actually happening in them. A door that opens in frame does not update any state. A character that falls gets back up because the model never tracked that it fell. This paper separates the problem into two halves: an explicit, programmable world state that a rules engine maintains, and a generative video model that renders what the state says should be visible. The starting observation is that today's interactive video models are prompted, not programmed. You can say "make the door open" and get a plausible clip, but there is no persistent rule governing when the door opens, what happens if you touch it twice, or whether it is still open when the camera pans away and comes back. The model has no memory of off-screen entities, no inventory, no task progress. For a multiplayer game engine or any long-horizon interactive experience, that is a dealbreaker. The authors argue you need a representation that is compact enough for a program to read and write, and structured enough to drive pixel-level visual generation. Their answer is the state-augmented 3D oriented bounding box. Every entity in the world is a 3D box with position, extent, and orientation in a shared coordinate system, augmented with persistent identity, semantic category, dynamic state, and appearance. No meshes, no skeletons, no pre-baked animations. item.title: WearableQA: A Benchmark for Health Reasoning over Real-World Wearable Data
item.description: By Ji Soo Lee, Xilun Chen, Pierce Chuang (Meta; KAIST; Korea University) WearableQA, a new benchmark for testing whether large language models can reason about real personal health data. Lead authors Ji Soo Lee, Xilun Chen, and Pierce Chuang, from Meta with collaborators at KAIST and Korea University, and Jason Wei among the senior contributors. The core idea is simple in motivation and hard in execution: give a model a real person's wearable sensor history, blood biomarkers, and demographics, and ask it multiple-choice questions that require reading the actual measurements rather than recalling medical trivia. The dataset is 4,084 questions built from the longitudinal records of 200 real users, and it deliberately preserves the noise and person-to-person variability of real wearable data. The benchmark is organized along two axes. The first is data reasoning versus health reasoning. Data reasoning means the answer must be derived directly from the numbers in front of you: compute a baseline, count excursions, estimate a recovery time. Health reasoning means applying medical knowledge to the data: assess risk, predict a phenotype, infer a fitness level. The second axis is single-signal versus cross-signal. Single-signal questions ask about one measurement in isolation. Cross-signal questions require relating two signals, like inferring what one measurement implies about another using the user's own history. There are 16 question types in total, and each is scored by exact match on a multiple-choice answer with ten options.

item.title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
item.description: By Yuqiao Tan, Shizhu He, Jun Zhao (Institute of Automation, CAS; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) SAEScientist-Bench, a new benchmark for testing whether AI agents can do autonomous interpretability research. Lead authors Yuqiao Tan, Shizhu He, and Jun Zhao, from the Key Laboratory of Cognitive Intelligence at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, with Kang Liu as the senior contributor. The motivation is a gap in the recursive self-improvement story. Most work on autonomous AI research automates the training pipeline: agents curate data, design algorithms, and run post-training. But they treat the model as a black box, judged only by external task scores. That leaves a missing pillar, which is the ability to look inside the model and audit what it actually learned. This benchmark measures that pillar, using Sparse Autoencoders as the tool. The setup is concrete. The model under test is Gemma 2, 9 billion, with Gemma Scope, a pretrained sparse autoencoder, attached to two layers of its residual stream. The SAE dictionary at each layer has 131,072 features. The agent is given a target concept, like Portuguese, or an earnings report, or a clinical symptom report, and its job is to design contrastive probes, texts that should activate the concept and texts that should not, and use those probes to navigate the dictionary and submit the single feature ID that best represents the concept. The feature is then scored on three axes against an expert reference feature pulled from Neuronpedia. item.title: Scores Alone Do Not Prove Discovery: The Discovery Certification Protocol for Auditing AI Research Agents
item.description: By Jingjie Ning, Shanshan Zhong, Xiaochuan Li (Carnegie Mellon University) The Discovery Certification Protocol, or DCP, a new framework for auditing whether an AI research agent actually discovered something, as opposed to getting a high score that a different, simpler process could have reached. Lead authors Jingjie Ning, Shanshan Zhong, and Xiaochuan Li, from the School of Computer Science at Carnegie Mellon University, with Ji Zeng as the senior contributor. The motivation is a real and growing problem. AI research agents now routinely report that they found a new algorithm, a better program, or a useful construction, and they back that up with a benchmark score. But a score, standing alone, does not tell you whether the agent did the work. It might have stumbled onto the answer through luck, or through a route that was already publicly available, or because the benchmark was leaky. The protocol asks three specific, measurable questions about one reported result, and it does so with pre-registered rules so that the audit cannot be gamed after the fact. The three questions are the whole design. Gate one asks whether the result is actually useful: does it beat a registered baseline by a minimum margin, measured on sealed evaluation data that was held back during the run? Gate two asks whether the outcome is recoverable without the agent's own research history. You give a fresh, matched agent the same starting information, the same tools, the same budget, and every web page the original agent saw, but you withhold the agent's internal run history, its hypotheses and trial results. If that fresh agent can still reach essentially the same score, then the discovery is not really a discovery; it was reachable from public and starting knowledge alone. item.title: DianShi-RxnDB: A Large-Scale Organic Reaction Data Platform
item.description: By Yubin Wang, Xingjian Wei, Jiang Wu (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; Fudan University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) DianShi-RxnDB, a new open database of organic chemistry reactions built specifically for both human researchers and AI agents. Lead authors Yubin Wang, Xingjian Wei, and Jiang Wu, from the Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, with collaborators at Fudan University and Shanghai Jiao Tong University. The premise is that a huge amount of synthetic chemistry knowledge is trapped in patent documents, scattered across text, images, and reaction schemes, and essentially unusable for computation. They built a fully automated pipeline that reads roughly 1.58 million patent documents and extracts about 24 million individual single-step reaction records out of them, each with the experimental detail a chemist or an agent would want. The pipeline is the story, and it is worth following step by step. They start with 20,256,438 raw patent records from the USPTO and EPO, covering organic synthesis patents from 1976 to 2025. They filter for organic chemistry relevance using the International Patent Classification codes, which cuts the pool to 2,512,925. Then they consolidate duplicates within each source, deduplicate across the USPTO and EPO, and drop records without usable full text. By the end, 1,580,939 patent documents enter the extraction stage, and 608,309 of them yield at least one reaction record that survives quality checks. The final database holds about 24 million reaction instances, of which about 14.8 million, roughly 61.7 percent, pass the automated qualification assessment. item.title: NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
item.description: By Guoliang Cao, Guohao Dai, Tianyu Guo (TokenRhythm Technologies; Infinigence AI; Tsinghua University) NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness. Lead authors Guoliang Cao, Guohao Dai, and Tianyu Guo, from a large alphabetical roster at TokenRhythm Technologies, Infinigence AI, Tsinghua University, Peking University, and The Chinese University of Hong Kong. This is a technical report for a family of agent-native models, and the framing question is recursive self-improvement: can a system observe its own capabilities and turn that evidence into the next round of training? The authors' claim is that you do not need exotic machinery to start this loop. A deployed routing harness - the execution layer that decides which model serves each request - already records three things on every turn: an execution trajectory, an estimate of capability demand, and an observable outcome. Their system couples a heterogeneous model pool with intelligent routing, converts those records into user-turn training examples, and feeds evaluation results back into the next training mixture. Here's how the data side works, because that's where most of the engineering lives. The corpus is on the order of 100000 to 1000000 harness-generated trajectories per the paper, a deliberately wide band. Each record goes through structural validation: the pipeline reconstructs requests, responses, tool calls, and observations, then checks payload readability, causal event order, and closure of tool-call result pairs. Trajectories are graded as complete, partially recoverable, or quarantined - missing responses and orphan tool observations get caught here. item.description: By Youngrok Park, Sangmin Bae, Hojung Jung (KAIST AI; Microsoft; University of Toronto; Mila, Université de Montréal) Eliciting Weak-to-Strong Generalization with On-Policy Reverse Distillation. First authors Youngrok Park and Sangmin Bae of KAIST AI, with Hojung Jung, and collaborators at Microsoft, the University of Toronto, and Mila at the Université de Montréal; Aaron Courville is a senior author. The question is weak-to-strong generalization: can a stronger student learn from a weaker teacher and end up surpassing it? Conventional distillation treats the weak teacher as an optimization target, which risks imposing the teacher's capacity ceiling on the student. On-policy distillation helps with the distribution mismatch but still matches the teacher's policy directly. This paper's method, OPRD - On-Policy Reverse Distillation - takes a different route: it never makes the teacher's policy a target. Instead it computes the direction of the teacher's policy shift, learned during weak-model post-training, and uses that direction only to rescale the student's own verifier-driven policy gradient. Mechanically: the teacher's policy shift relative to its reference policy gives a unit direction at each token. The student's policy gradient is decomposed into a component along that direction and an orthogonal remainder. The used update is the original gradient plus a nonnegative scale lambda times the projected component - so the projected part is amplified by one plus lambda and the orthogonal part passes through untouched. Because this map is invertible for nonnegative lambda, two properties hold: stationarity is preserved, the transformed gradient is zero exactly when the original is zero, and the inner product of original and transformed gradients is at least the original gradient's squared norm, with the extra term being lambda times the squared alignment coefficient. item.title: Omni Interaction Agent Technical Report
item.description: By Orantqing, Shengpeng Ji, Junlong Tong (Tencent Hunyuan Speech Team; Zhejiang University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University) The Omni Interaction Agent Technical Report, presenting Gander. Lead contributors from the Tencent Hunyuan Speech Team, with Zhejiang University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, and Nanyang Technological University. Gander is an end-to-end model that tries to unify three things in one system: continuous multimodal perception across video, speech, and text; real-time full-duplex interaction where users can interrupt at any time; and agentic task execution. The report's first argument is architectural rather than empirical: true interactivity cannot be layered on top of a turn-based model with a voice activity detector. Pipelines built on VAD plus ASR handle request-response fine but struggle with hesitation, pauses, barge-in interruptions, overlapping speech, backchannels, and noisy multi-party scenes. Their answer is to make interaction state part of the model's own prediction - the model explicitly decides whether to listen or speak at each step of a streaming sequence. Gander's central design is a Brain-Cerebellum split. The cerebellum is a streaming real-time interaction model running a Thinker-Talker architecture: streaming video and audio encoders feed a language backbone that operates over flattened one-second chunks, and a fast speech decoder renders audio. The Brain is a separate, heavier reasoning module - deliberately training-free and plug-and-play - that the cerebellum invokes through tool calls for long-horizon work like coding or file operations; the Brain's results come back asynchronously and the cerebellum folds them into the ongoing conversation. item.title: GE-Act 2.0: Pretraining and Scaling a World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation
item.description: By AgiBot Research Team (AgiBot Research) GE-Act 2.0: Pretraining and Scaling a World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation, from the AgiBot Research Team. The lineage here is the Genie Envisioner line. Most world-action models inherit a pretrained video generator; this report's distinguishing choice is that every trainable generative and action component is initialized from scratch on manipulation data, and the central empirical question is how much zero-shot, out-of-distribution capability you can buy with data scale alone, without task-specific fine-tuning. The system has three components. First, CoAE, a control-oriented autoencoder. Standard video autoencoders downsample eight or sixteen times per axis and are trained for reconstruction. CoAE uses a 64-fold spatial downsampling, mapping a 256 by 384 frame to a 4 by 6 grid of 512-channel latents - 24 tokens per frame. It initializes from the 128-channel DC-AE with expanded width, and trains with pixel, perceptual, and adversarial reconstruction plus alignment to three frozen teachers: SigLIP for language-aligned semantics, V-JEPA 2.1 for spatiotemporal structure, and DINOv3 for dense features. Probes show why this matters: with the same two-layer inverse-dynamics probe, CoAE gets an action mean-absolute-error of 0.01673, within 13 to 31 percent of DINOv3 and V-JEPA which use sixteen times as many tokens per frame, while DC-AE at the same compression is 54 percent worse and SigLIP 88 percent worse.

item.title: AuK Technical Report: An Open-Source Foundational Model for Speech Generation and Editing
item.description: By Ziyang Ma, Zhikang Niu, Wenming Tu (AuK open-source research institution) The AuK Technical Report: an open-source foundational model for speech generation and editing, with a distilled variant called AuK-Flash. It comes from the AuK open-source research institution; first authors Ziyang Ma, Zhikang Niu, and Wenming Tu lead that release. AuK unifies five task families under one interface - a natural-language instruction plus optional audio context mapped to a target waveform: speech generation, content editing, enhancement and separation, paralinguistic editing, and acoustic editing. The training corpus is about 3.03 billion instruction-audio instances covering 1.95 million hours of effective audio supervision. Architecture, in three parts. The semantic side uses a multimodal LLM encoder based on Qwen2.5-Omni that processes text alone or text with reference audio and fuses hierarchical hidden states into one semantic condition via a learned per-layer weighting. The acoustic side is the AuK-VAE, trained jointly on speech, general audio, and music at 24 kilohertz, with a normalizing-flow-regularized posterior; it provides both reference-conditioning latents and the output space - 64-dimensional latents at 50 hertz. The backbone is roughly 1.5 billion parameters: 10 dual-stream MMDiT blocks followed by 20 single-stream DiT blocks, hidden dimension 1536, 24 heads, a SwiGLU feed-forward with 3072 intermediate units, predicting rectified-flow velocity over the VAE latent. Dual-stream blocks preserve separate semantic and acoustic residual pathways before fusion; single-stream blocks refine jointly.

item.title: Reason Through the Latent! Making Latent Visual Reasoning Necessary
item.description: By Suhyeong Park, Junha Jung, Jaewoo Kang (Korea University; AIGEN Sciences) Reason Through the Latent! Making Latent Visual Reasoning Necessary, by Suhyeong Park, Junha Jung, and Jaewoo Kang of Korea University and AIGEN Sciences. On the topology standing rule, this one is squarely a recurrent-depth latent chain-of-thought paper for multimodal models. The premise: latent visual reasoning does computation in hidden states instead of explicit textual chains of thought. Nobody usually checks whether the model actually depends on those hidden states. The authors point out the confound bluntly: if the original multimodal context remains anywhere in the network, whatever latent path you added is decorative and can be bypassed. Two diagnostic experiments start it. First, weak behavioral reliance: on existing latent visual reasoners, replacing the latent content with a blank-image latent, a matched latent from a different-answer example, or norm-matched noise changes accuracy by almost nothing - one cited method shifts at most half a percentage point across all three replacements - because the normal multimodal answer context is still available. Second, where does pretrained visual competence live? Passing intermediate-layer states of the frozen vision-language model alone into the same frozen upper decoder, the full multimodal question state reaches 75.9 percent on V-star, the multimodal question rows alone reach 75.4, while a text-only question state bottoms out at 35.6 and adding raw visual features to the text-only state recovers nothing. So the competence is already integrated into the question representation, and it isn't reconstructable from raw visual features.

item.title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By Zhiwei Zhang, Zechen Sun, Fei Zhao (AllSpark Team) Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation, by Zhiwei Zhang, Zechen Sun, and Fei Zhao, from the AllSpark Team. On-policy distillation is the post-training recipe where a student model samples its own rollouts and a frozen, stronger teacher provides dense token-level supervision through a mode-seeking reverse KL objective. It can reach teacher-level accuracy roughly an order of magnitude faster than reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, but it has a structural blind spot: the teacher's supervision is admitted on every prompt without ever checking whether the teacher is actually right on that prompt. This paper's argument is that reverse KL is mode-seeking, so a confidently wrong teacher induces a strong, misleading update, and that existing fixes — entropy, teacher-student likelihood agreement, token trust regions — measure uncertainty or agreement, not correctness. Figure 2 in the paper is the motivating diagnostic: on code, teacher self-confidence separates reliable from unreliable prompts at an AUROC of only 0.51, versus 0.73 on math, and in the low-reliability regime the teacher's highest-confidence sampled response is wrong 84 percent of the time on code and 61 percent on math. That is exactly the error mode uniform on-policy distillation propagates. The proposed method, TGOPD, is a hard per-prompt gate. Before admitting dense supervision, the teacher generates K-T probe rollouts on the same prompt while the student is still decoding — K-T equals 3 in the main experiments — a verifier scores them, and their pass rate becomes the reliability estimate. If at least two of three probes pass, the prompt gets the full dense OPD signal. item.title: EmbodiedSkills: A Unified Framework for Orchestrating, Training, and Deploying VLA Agents
item.description: By Wei Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Yutong Lin (Zhejiang University; Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Cornell University) EmbodiedSkills: A Unified Framework for Orchestrating, Training, and Deploying VLA Agents, by Wei Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, and Yutong Lin, from Zhejiang University, with collaborators at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Cornell University, National University of Singapore, Hangzhou DEEP Robotics, and Universal Ubiquitous AI. Vision-language-action models map camera images and an instruction directly to robot actions, and recent policies are good at that mapping. The paper's point is that long-horizon manipulation needs more than action prediction: an agent has to perceive, plan, check that a proposed skill is even valid in the current state, execute, verify what actually happened, and recover when it goes wrong. An action chunk issued by a VLA policy does not, by itself, guarantee that the operation is executable in the current state or that anyone checks the outcome. EmbodiedSkills is an agent-layer framework that treats every skill decision as an execution proposal: a guarded runtime validates prerequisites before execution, verifies outcomes afterward, and logs the whole loop as structured trajectories you can trace and train on. The architecture is a closed-loop AgentLoop with six phases — observe, plan, preflight, execute, verify, and recover — wrapped around a shared skill interface, with a strict separation between what the policy proposes and what the runtime permits. The high-level policy is a Qwen3-VL model that receives a deployment-consistent compact context: the task, current phase, available task artifacts, and a bounded, compressed summary of the loop history; raw simulator internals are never admitted into the policy context. item.description: By Zixun Huang, Kishan Panaganti, Haitao Mi (Tencent HY LLM Frontier; University of Pennsylvania) FlowBalance: Verifier-Grounded Self-Improvement from On-Policy Reasoning Experience, by Zixun Huang, Kishan Panaganti, and Haitao Mi, from Tencent HY LLM Frontier and the University of Pennsylvania. The problem the paper takes on is the standard self-improvement loop for reasoning models: sample a group of solutions, verify them, update the policy. Two failure modes make that loop fragile. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards supplies one terminal scalar for a response that may contain thousands of tokens, so the supervision is reliable but sparse. The complementary signal — a frozen copy of the same policy, conditioned on training-only privileged context like a reference solution, scoring the already-sampled tokens — is dense and cheap, but it is not trustworthy: because that hindsight view sees information unavailable at inference, it can favor a plausible trajectory that the verifier rejects, shorten reasoning, or concentrate the update on one narrow solution mode. Blindly following it creates self-confirmation, where the model's own erroneous preference becomes the next update's supervision. FlowBalance answers a distributional question: given sparse verified outcomes and dense but imperfect self-guidance, what normalized distribution over complete responses should the next policy learn? The mechanics are worth stating precisely because they are what you would implement. For a prompt and its rollout group of N responses, compute stopped group-relative verifier advantages from the reward mean and standard deviation of the group. item.title: What Else Needs Fixing? Exploring Cost-Effective Test-Time Compute for Revision Propagation in Artifacts Generated Through Conversation
item.description: By Daisuke Kikuta (NTT) What Else Needs Fixing? Exploring Cost-Effective Test-Time Compute for Revision Propagation in Artifacts Generated Through Conversation, by Daisuke Kikuta, from NTT. The setting is the one every assistant product lives in: a user and a language model build an artifact — an itinerary, an invoice, a project schedule, a bill of materials — through conversation, and then the user asks for a local change. Remove destination B. The model must not only remove B; it must find every dependency and propagate the revision: shift the schedule because the removed stop anchored the day, recompute the budget because per-person pricing changes with the count. The dependenices here are implicit — embedded in the conversation history, not in a call graph or a knowledge graph — which is what distinguishes this from repository-level coding, knowledge-editing ripple effects, and document editing, where dependencies are explicit or statically analyzable. The paper introduces RevPropBench, a benchmark for exactly this setting, and evaluates nine revision methods across six models to find the most cost-effective use of test-time compute. The benchmark construction is the part worth understanding before critiquing the numbers. Fifty scenarios across nine domains — travel itineraries, invoices, shopping carts, project schedules, course plans, data pipelines, deployment configurations, organizational access plans, and manufacturing bills of materials — covering six propagation patterns, including the temporal cascade, threshold gating, and reference updates. Each scenario is instantiated at three artifact sizes, ten, fifty, and one hundred JSON elements, for 150 samples; a seed-forty-two split holds out 10 scenarios as development data and reports on the remaining 120. item.title: Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier
item.description: By Ziyuan Liu, Hengqi Liu, Zichuan Wang (AllSpark Team) Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier, by Ziyuan Liu, Hengqi Liu, and Zichuan Wang, from the AllSpark team. This is a search-agent report, not a new foundation model, but it is the top paper on today's feed by a wide margin, and it matters for anyone building agents that have to work from incomplete information. The team presents Iris-mini and Iris-pro, two search agents trained at 35 billion and 397 billion total parameters, both mixture-of-experts with 256,000 token context windows, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B respectively. The headline claim is an end-to-end recipe: data construction, training, and evaluation for web search agents, with results reported under a controlled protocol that separates the policy from the inference harness. The problem setup is that search agents have to do more than reason. They have to decide what to search for, how to interpret retrieved evidence, when to keep exploring, and when the evidence is good enough to answer. Two structural issues motivate the design. First, naturally occurring web questions are too easy for training: a model can answer many of them from parametric memory. Second, the team argues, and this is the through-line of the whole report, that inference-time context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most of the reported differences between systems. Long search sessions exhaust the context window before the agent has resolved all its constraints, so the effective search budget ends up much smaller than the nominal context length. Reporting scores under one context-management strategy can therefore obscure how much of the performance is the policy and how much is the surrounding harness.

item.title: Motion-Omni: End-to-End Joint Speech and Full-Body Motion for Spoken Dialogue
item.description: By Chengqian Ma, Wei Tao, Haoyu Zhang (Peking University, LIGHTSPEED, The Chinese University of Hong Kong Shenzhen, Independent Researcher) Motion-Omni: End-to-End Joint Speech and Full-Body Motion for Spoken Dialogue, by Chengqian Ma, Wei Tao, and Haoyu Zhang, from Peking University, LIGHTSPEED, and the Chinese University of Hong Kong Shenzhen, with the corresponding author as an independent researcher. The question this paper asks is whether full-body motion can be a native output of a spoken dialogue model, generated from the same hidden states that produce the speech, instead of the standard cascade where a dialogue model first generates the response and a separate motion model then runs a second full inference pass over the finished audio. The cascade has two structural costs: the second pass, and the fact that no motion objective can ever update the speech or dialogue parameters. The framework has four components: a Speech Projector, an LLM backbone, a Speech Generator, and a Part-Aware Motion Generator. The speech pathway is conventional in spirit, an LLM that emits discrete speech units at 12.5 hertz, passed through a generator that renders them to a waveform. The interesting interface is between the speech generator and the motion generator. The motion generator attends to the speech generator's hidden states as keys and values, and consumes the embeddings of the emitted speech tokens as queries, interpolated from the 12.5 hertz speech-unit rate up to the 30 hertz motion rate. Motion is thus generated directly from the representations that produce the speech, with no rendered waveform as an intermediate input, and it covers explicit facial expression plus hand, upper-body, and lower-body motion. The rate mismatch between the two outputs is the core architectural problem, and this dual-input conditioning is how it is bridged.

item.title: WorldSculpt: Generating Compositional Worlds from Grounded Videos
item.description: By Muyao Niu, Jixuan He, Ruihan Yu (Alaya Lab, The University of Tokyo) WorldSculpt: Generating Compositional Worlds from Grounded Videos, by Muyao Niu, Jixuan He, and Ruihan Yu, from Alaya Lab and the University of Tokyo. The problem is generating a compositional 3D representation of a cluttered real scene containing hundreds of objects, where the output is a collection of individual object meshes placed in a shared world frame, rather than a fused mesh or a point cloud of Gaussians. The motivation is practical: downstream applications like gaming, AR and VR, simulation, and robotics do not consume an undifferentiated soup of surface geometry. They need each chair and vase to be a separate mesh that can be selected, moved, and re-simulated on its own. The tension in the prior work is clean to state. Geometry-centric methods, per-scene optimization, feed-forward volumetric or Gaussian regressors, pointmap models, recover accurate geometry in the observed regions but reconstruct the scene as a single fused representation and leave incomplete geometry wherever occlusion hides it. Generative priors offer the complementary strength: they learn a distribution over plausible 3D content and can infer coherent geometry beyond the visible evidence, but existing ones either process the whole scene jointly and still output a monolithic representation, or model a complete individual object from a single pose-free image, which does not jointly condition on a consistent set of views or generate in a known scene coordinate frame. The paper's claim is that a complex scene with hundreds of objects can be generated compositionally by adapting a strong single-object 3D generative prior to multi-view observations.

item.title: Ask Before You Optimize: Dynamic Pre-Formulation Clarification for Interactive Optimization
item.description: By Sihan Ge, Yichen Lin, Chenyu Zhou (Cardinal Operations, Shanghai Jiao Tong University) Ask Before You Optimize: Dynamic Pre-Formulation Clarification for Interactive Optimization, by Sihan Ge, Yichen Lin, and Chenyu Zhou, from Cardinal Operations and Shanghai Jiao Tong University. This paper carves out a specific failure mode in LLM-based operations research and treats it as a standalone task: the case where a user describes a business problem in natural language but leaves out the facts that actually determine the structure of the optimization model. A user may state capacities and demands without specifying the objective, or give a routing rule without saying whether the time windows are hard or soft. Those omissions are not superficial. In a vehicle-routing example the paper uses, if a user omits whether a courier must return to the origin, an agent that silently assumes a closed tour changes the constraint structure without asking. The paper's central observation is that most evaluations of LLM optimization agents assume a complete specification and measure whether the agent can solve or express a given model, skipping the earlier question of whether the available information even supports a meaningful formulation. Strong LLM agents, the authors find, often declare readiness while core business facts remain unclarified, or silently fill missing facts with unsupported defaults. The task they define is pre-formulation clarification: determine whether the current public specification is model-ready, and when it is not, recover the missing formulation-critical facts with as little interaction as possible. A fact is formulation-critical if its value can change the structure of the resulting optimization formulation.

item.title: Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference
item.description: By Mostafa Elhoushi, Alex Pretko, Nolan Dey (Cerebras Systems, MBZUAI) Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference, by Mostafa Elhoushi, Alex Pretko, and Nolan Dey, from Cerebras Systems and MBZUAI. The paper's thesis is that layer dropout, also called stochastic depth, should be part of state-of-the-art LLM pre-training, and that the prior evidence against it came from suboptimal configurations rather than from a fundamental limitation. The context is that dropout of all kinds has largely disappeared from large-scale LLM recipes: models are trained for a single epoch over massive datasets, there is little opportunity for classical overfitting, and the empirical literature reports that activation dropout degrades performance under these conditions. Layer dropout is different in kind from activation dropout, and that difference is the whole argument. The specific claim is that with the right distribution of sparsity across depth, the right temporal schedule, and the right optimizer hyperparameters, layer dropout at the same training FLOPs leads to lower loss, and for a fixed number of steps the model reaches lower or similar validation loss while saving up to 25 percent of training FLOPs. The second, arguably more important claim is that the same mechanism buys post-training inference optimizations: early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding, yielding up to a 1.5 times inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss. All of this is established across more than 2,400 training experiments, spanning models from 271 million to 8.2 billion parameters and datasets up to 160 billion tokens, all run on Cerebras CS-3 systems. The configuration space is broken into three axes, and the ablations isolate each one. The depth distribution has three candidates: uniform, where every layer has the same dropout rate;

item.title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs
item.description: By Shangkun Wang, Nina Cai, Charles Hong (Google, Google DeepMind) MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs, by Shangkun Wang, Nina Cai, and Charles Hong, from Google and Google DeepMind. The paper presents a multi-agent system for automating TPU kernel engineering, benchmarked on JAXBench, a suite of 50 diverse kernel tasks built from real workloads of state-of-the-art open-source models, plus production kernels where hand-tuned references exist. The headline numbers: a 1.58 times geometric mean speedup across the full JAXBench workloads, and on the eight production kernels with human-written baselines, a 2.32 times geometric mean speedup for the best agent configuration against 2.02 times for the human hand-tuned code. The framework is released as open source under the accelerator-agents repository. The motivation is that TPU kernel work is painstakingly manual. Accelerator APIs are rigid, memory constraints are strict, compiler errors are opaque, and even functionally correct code needs iterative empirical profiling to reach peak performance. Compiler frameworks like Halide, TVM, and Ansor decouple algorithms from scheduling but still demand domain expertise or expensive evolutionary search. LLM-based approaches help, but standard zero-shot or few-shot generation falls short without real-time compiler feedback and profiling in the loop. The architecture is a shared pool of specialized sub-agents orchestrated three different ways. The sub-agents are: a planning agent that writes a high-level algorithmic optimization plan from the hardware specs and the reference implementation; an implementation agent that translates the plan into valid Pallas code, with an iterative compile-fix loop that interprets compiler feedback and resolves errors before execution; a test synthesis agent that builds test suites and an execution agent that runs them on the target hardware

item.title: LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes
item.description: By Chuyan Chen, Haoxing Chen, Kun Chen (Inclusion AI) LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes, by Chuyan Chen, Haoxing Chen, and Kun Chen, from the AGI Research Center at Inclusion AI. This one is here both because it has the day's highest true upvote count and because it lands under the standing rule for foundation-model releases: it is a new image-generation base model trained from scratch, and it ships open, which is the part that makes it worth your time rather than just another leaderboard entry. The framing. The paper pairs two things that do not usually get paired this cleanly. One side is a 6 billion parameter Diffusion Transformer, a DiT, trained from scratch as the generation engine. The other side is a frozen vision-language understanding module built on the LLaDA 2.0 Mini diffusion language model backbone, which supplies the semantic and instruction-following prior. The two are coupled so that the understanding module conditions the generation, rather than the generation model trying to learn its own text comprehension from scratch. The key design decision is about data ordering: instead of leaning heavily on paired image-text data from the very start, the authors first build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training, and only then move to paired image-text supervised fine-tuning. The stated motivation is that a model that has already learned to generate plausible images from images alone does not have to burn its capacity learning basic visual structure from scratch on the paired data.

item.title: LatentPress: Context Compression Beyond Text and Vision
item.description: By Zhengze Zhou, Hejian Sang (Cornell University, Iowa State University) LatentPress: Context Compression Beyond Text and Vision, by Zhengze Zhou and Hejian Sang, from Cornell University and Iowa State University. This is a small, focused paper on a specific infrastructure problem, and the idea is a clean one: stop carrying compressed context as human-readable text or as rendered images that have to be decoded, and instead write it directly into a third representation, continuous memory tokens that a frozen language model reads straight through its input-embedding interface. If you are building long-context or agentic systems where you compress history to fit the context window, this is a proposal to compress into the model's own latent space rather than into a format you then have to decode back out. The motivation is that the consumer of compressed context is usually a language model, yet the compressed context is almost always produced in a format meant for a human. You either summarize the history into readable text, or you render it into an image and let the model OCR or decode it. Both routes add a decoding step the model did not ask for, and both lose information in the process. Text summaries are cheap to produce but throw away the fine-grained detail a memory task depends on, and image-based compression is more faithful but pays a decoding cost and inherits the OCR error floor. LatentPress's argument is that if the reader is a model, the writer should write in the model's native representation. So the system writes conversational histories and long documents into continuous memory tokens, and the frozen decoder reads those tokens directly through its input-embedding interface, with no text reconstruction at inference time. The result is a third representation that is neither text nor image, but the internal form the model already speaks.

item.title: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM
item.description: By Sergii Kozyrev, Davyd Maiboroda (Minima AI) Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization, by Sergii Kozyrev and Davyd Maiboroda, from Minima AI. This is a short, focused systems paper rather than a model release, and its whole argument rests on one counterintuitive claim: the recurrent half of a hybrid large language model is the easier half to quantize, not the harder half. If you are running hybrid models like Qwen 3.8 27B and you have been hand-tuning which blocks to keep in high precision, the paper says the hand-tuning is backwards. The setup. Hybrid large language models interleave ordinary softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet. Gated DeltaNet keeps a recurrent state that summarizes the whole context in a fixed size, which is what makes it cheap to run over long sequences. The catch that has guided the community so far is that a recurrence is supposed to accumulate error. Every small mistake in the state gets carried forward and compounded over thousands of steps, so people assumed the Gated DeltaNet block, especially its decay gate and its write-strength gate, had to stay in 8-bit or 16-bit precision no matter what. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen 3.8 27B, which has 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 attention layers, all left the Gated DeltaNet block in 8 or 16 bits on exactly that intuition. The decay gate in particular was treated as sacred, on the reasoning that a small bias in the decay rate is a small change every single step, and over 32K steps a small per-step bias becomes a large state drift.

item.title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
item.description: By Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, Wenting Zhao (Salesforce AI Research, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning, by Heng Wang, Jielin Qiu, and Wenting Zhao, from Salesforce AI Research and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. This is a result that sounds like a joke until you check the numbers: the paper argues that the scoring function at the heart of every KV-cache eviction method contributes almost nothing, and that evicting tokens uniformly at random within each attention head matches the best prior evictor while being much faster to serve. If you have built a KV-cache compressor, this paper is proposing you delete your scorer. The problem. Large language models do their best work on tasks that require extended reasoning, and the way they do it is by generating long chains of thought. Long chains of thought make the KV cache a severe memory bottleneck, because every token the model reasons over stays in the cache and has to be attended to. The standard response in the literature is a shared paradigm: score each cached token by some estimate of how much it will matter later, and keep the top-scoring ones. Methods like SnapKV and VaSE are built on exactly this idea, and they invest real engineering in the scoring function, whether that is an attention-magnitude heuristic, a learned importance estimator, or a redundancy-aware variant. The paper's opening claim is that this selection signal, the whole reason those methods exist, is doing almost no work, and it frames the question as an empirical one that the field has not actually checked: everyone assumes the scorer is the point, but nobody has run the obvious control experiment of evicting at random and measuring the gap.

item.title: Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models II: One Training Example
item.description: By Zixuan Fu, Bingxiang He, Yuxin Zuo (Tsinghua University, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Northeastern University) Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models, Part Two: One Training Example, by Zixuan Fu, Bingxiang He, and Yuxin Zuo, from Tsinghua University, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and Northeastern University, with collaborators at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Johns Hopkins. This is a data-efficiency paper that pushes a familiar training method to its most extreme limit and finds something surprising: on-policy distillation, which is usually run on a full dataset of examples, keeps improving for hundreds of steps when you train it on a single query. The paper's argument is that on-policy distillation is not data-hungry the way supervised fine-tuning is, and that the bottleneck has always been the optimization, not the data. The setup. On-policy distillation, or OPD, combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher. The student produces its own sequences, and the teacher scores each token, so the student is always being corrected on the states it actually visits rather than on a fixed dataset of target sequences. This is the property that separates OPD from ordinary supervised fine-tuning: in SFT the student imitates a fixed set of target trajectories, so the data you give it is exactly the states it will see, but in OPD the student explores its own trajectory distribution and the teacher's supervision lands on states the student would actually visit in deployment. Prior work has studied the algorithmic side of this, the loss, the sampling, the token-level signal, but the paper says the role of the training data itself has been left unclear. item.title: Puffin-World: Scaling a Unified Multimodal Model with Native 3D World States
item.description: By Kang Liao, Yihang Luo, Xiao-Ming Wu (S-Lab, Nanyang Technological University, University of Michigan, Beijing Jiaotong University) Puffin-World: Scaling a Unified Multimodal Model with Native 3D World States, by Kang Liao, Yihang Luo, and Xiao-Ming Wu, from S-Lab at Nanyang Technological University, the University of Michigan, and Beijing Jiaotong University, with collaborators at ACE Robotics. This one is here under the standing rule for foundation-model releases, because it is a new unified multimodal model, a single architecture that does scene and physics understanding, free-viewpoint spatial generation, and 3D world generation and reconstruction, all from one set of weights. It is the kind of base-model release the rule is meant to catch, and it ships open with code, models, and datasets. The central design decision is that the model works in what the paper calls native 3D world states, rather than treating 3D as something you reconstruct as a post-processing step. The framework jointly models three native states: physics, which is a gravity field and a latitude map; geometry, which is depth; and appearance, which is the image itself. On top of those three it uses a unified representation the authors call Omni-Camera, which is meant to support diverse tasks and flexible camera motions within one representation rather than a different parameterization per task. The motivation is that a lot of prior work keeps the 3D understanding, the simulation, and the generation as separate modules that you have to stitch together offline, and the paper's argument is that keeping them native and unified in one model is what lets the same architecture do understanding, generation, and reconstruction coherently.

item.title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
item.description: By Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley (Microsoft Research; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) StudentSim, by Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, and Michel Galley, from Microsoft Research, with co-authors from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The paper's argument in one line: if you want to train and evaluate adaptive AI tutors, you need a scalable source of per-student feedback, and the way to get it is to train a small language model to be that student. The setting is concrete. An AI tutor is only as good as the feedback it gets about which guidance helps which student, and collecting that feedback from real learners is slow, expensive, and sparse. The authors define two properties a student simulator must have. Behavioral fidelity, which they call F: does the simulator reproduce the student's own responses, including the characteristic mistakes? And guidance responsiveness, which they call R: given the student's wrong response and a tutor's correction, does the simulator update toward the corrected response? The two are deliberately separable. A faithful simulator that ignores guidance is useless for training a tutor; a responsive one that does not start from the student's actual competence is a different student. The prior art splits into three lines, and none of them hits both properties at once. Cognitive-state and behavior-prediction models, like knowledge tracing and human-play move predictors, match learner behavior at the population level but have no input channel for natural-language guidance, so they cannot be a reward for a tutor that talks. LLM-prompted student simulators condition on a textual competence description and converse, which scales, but a thin text description is a weak conditioning channel, and a growing validity-focused literature raises architectural and fidelity concerns about exactly that recipe. item.title: SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers
item.description: By Shaowen Wang, Ge Zhang, Kairong Luo (Tsinghua University; ByteDance Seed; M-A-P; TokenWave.AI) SMELT: Scaling Laws for Compute-Matched MoE Looped Transformers, by Shaowen Wang, Ge Zhang, and Kairong Luo of Tsinghua University, ByteDance Seed, M-A-P, and TokenWave AI, with further authors from those labs. Looped transformers repeat a shared block of layers instead of stacking new ones, and the pitch is seductive: reasoning depth without extra parameters, with looped models matching or beating unlooped models several times their size on arithmetic and math. But there is a catch the literature mostly waves away: looping a twelve-layer model to twenty-four executed layers stores half the weights yet spends roughly a twenty-four-layer model's compute per token and needs its full key-value cache. Most prior evaluations hold parameter count fixed and let compute float, so the reported gains conflate an architectural advantage with uncontrolled extra computation. This paper is, by its own accounting, the first multi-scale study to hold all three budgets fixed at once, per-token FLOPs, total non-embedding parameters, and KV cache, and it still finds looping wins, which makes it the most convincing evidence yet that depth reuse is real. Mixture-of-experts architectures are what make honest matching feasible. When looping costs extra FLOPs, the recipe narrows the hidden dimension; because MoE decouples total parameters from per-token compute, it then recovers the lost capacity by raising the expert count rather than giving it up; and KV cache parity is restored separately through head size and grouped-query-attention ratio, with every matched pair within four percent on FLOPs, one percent on parameters, and four percent on cache. item.title: UI-Venus-2 Technical Report
item.description: By Venus Team, Zhuohan Cai, Haoxing Chen (Ant Group) UI-Venus-2 Technical Report, by the Venus Team with Zhuohan Cai and Haoxing Chen, from Ant Group. This one lands under the standing rule for a reason: it is a technical report introducing a new general-purpose foundation GUI agent, and it is open-sourced, which is the part that matters most if you want to reproduce or build on it. The framing is practical, not speculative. GUI agents have moved fast on grounding and navigation benchmarks, but the authors argue that benchmark-oriented models do not transfer to dependable real-world use for three specific reasons. Environment coverage is too narrow to span multilingual mobile ecosystems, dynamic websites, and full desktop operating systems. Task construction is brittle, because generated queries often are not grounded in what an application can actually do. And the verification that supplies RL reward is unreliable, because a coarse verifier confuses partial progress with true completion, misses task-critical visual evidence, or exposes a reward a policy can exploit. The paper's design principle is that these three dimensions must be scaled jointly, not treated as independent knobs. The system is a unified closed-loop reasoning-and-action agent. Given a natural-language instruction, it observes rendered interface images, reasons about the task state, executes an action, and folds the resulting environmental feedback into the next decision. Two model sizes ship, a 9B and a 27B, both initialized from open-source Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B multimodal foundations. The action space is extended with desktop-specific actions so the same policy can operate on a phone, a browser, and an OS.

item.title: ZimaBlue: Evolving Generalizable World Action Models through Scalable Video Pre-training
item.description: By Xionghao Wu, Yijun Yang, Shiyang Zhou (Joy Future Academy) ZimaBlue is from Joy Future Academy, and the lead authors are Xionghao Wu, Yijun Yang, and Shiyang Zhou. It is a framework for building World Action Models, or WAMs, from large-scale video, and the central empirical claim is a scaling result: on real-robot zero-shot evaluation, going from target-robot data alone to over 120,000 hours of embodied video lifts task success from 36.1 percent to 77.8 percent. That is a big gap, and it is the whole argument in one sentence. The paper is a three-stage training framework, plus a deployment architecture, built to turn that gap into a practical system. The idea is to use each data source for its natural role. Stage one, video pre-training, learns causal visual dynamics from a huge corpus of first-person and robot egocentric video, with no action labels at all, starting from a generic text-to-video diffusion transformer called Wan2.2-TI2V-5B. Stage two, video-action mid-training, grounds those visual dynamics in actual robot control by introducing multi-embodiment robot trajectories with synchronized observations, proprioceptive states, language instructions, and actions, using a unified cross-embodiment action interface. Stage three, post-training, specializes the model to a single deployment embodiment and its action space, and this is where the fast branch enters. The unifying piece is the World Action Model itself, or WAM. Instead of a reactive policy that maps observation straight to action, a WAM jointly models how the visual world will evolve and what the robot should do within that evolution, with a single generative objective. The authors are explicit about why they do not just initialize from an off-the-shelf video generator.
