item.title: Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering
item.description: By Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, Wook-Shin Han (POSTECH) Hi-Q is from POSTECH, and the authors are Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, and Wook-Shin Han. It is a framework for multi-hop question answering that reframes the core difficulty as something specific: the granularity at which a question is expressed is usually different from the granularity at which the evidence for it is retrievable. The motivation is a single example they reuse throughout. When was the start of the battle of the birthplace of the performer of III? Answering that requires first identifying the performer of III, then that person's birthplace, and finally the start date of the battle at that location. One surface sentence, three dependent retrieval steps. The existing three families of methods each handle the mismatch in a way that misses when a query unit is already answerable. Single retrieval issues the coarse question once and hopes the top passages cover the whole chain. Graph RAG builds a fixed corpus-side structure before any query arrives, so the granularity is query-agnostic. Iterative retrieval adapts the query over time, but never tests whether the reformulation it just issued was actually supported by evidence, so an early wrong bridge propagates forward. Hi-Q's core idea is to make the decomposition decision evidence-conditioned rather than template-driven. It grows a query tree online. At each node, a resolution operator retrieves the top passages for the current query unit and has a retrieval-grounded reader try to answer from them. If the reader produces a real answer, the node is resolved and the branch terminates. If the reader returns nothing, the node is unresolved and becomes eligible for refinement. So the tree's topology is determined by corpus support signals, not by a fixed decomposition template or a pre-built graph.

item.title: DroneCATS: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs as Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agents for Drone Control
item.description: By Jaewoo Park, Minyoung Lee, Sukmin Seo (NAVER Cloud) DroneCATS, from Jaewoo Park, Minyoung Lee, and Sukmin Seo, among the NAVER Cloud drone AI team. This is a benchmark and a reference agent for putting a multimodal large language model directly inside a drone's control loop. The question is what happens when you stop engineering responsibility out of the model. Recent systems that fly drones with an MLLM almost all subtract: TypeFly keeps the model as a planner over detections, See Point Fly reduces control to pointing at a pixel, Fly0 confines the model to grounding and hands trajectory generation to a separate planner, and OnFly adds a verifier that corrects the model before its output reaches the actuators. Each takes something away and then reports that it works. But that workflow varies the system and holds the model fixed, so it can answer how much the model can do once you remove parts of the job, not which parts of embodied drone control actually depend on the model. DroneCATS asks the converse. It holds the agent fixed and varies the model, so the backbone is the independent variable. The agent is deliberately minimal. It is a model-agnostic wrapper in which the entire action space is declared in natural language in the prompt, with no fine-tuning, no action head, and no function-calling schema. The model is a swappable component, and swapping it changes nothing else around it. It works at a high level on four primitives. The first is go, which carries a pixel and a depth estimate, and a rule-based controller back-projects that pair into a three-dimensional displacement and hands it to the flight stack as a velocity setpoint. The model never emits a velocity or an attitude. The second is rotate, an in-place yaw, which is the only way to look for a target that is out of frame. item.title: Safin-1: Safety from Within through Memory-Native State Evolution
item.description: By Ming Zhang, Kaisen Yang, Shu Yu (Shanghai AI Laboratory) Safin-1, from the Safin team at Shanghai AI Laboratory, with Ming Zhang, Kaisen Yang, and Shu Yu among the contributors. This is an architecture paper that asks whether safety can live inside a model's own computation rather than being bolted on as an external constraint. The starting point is a distinction most alignment work quietly blurs. A language model retains context in one substrate, a token-level cache or a recurrent state, but it encodes reusable behaviors like safety in a different one, model updates, adapters, or learned prefixes imposed at inference time. The paper's claim is that these should be the same substrate. It calls the principle Safety from Within: safety-relevant capabilities should be represented and invoked through the model's native computation, not through post-hoc alignment that depends on external safeguards. The mechanism is a new architecture called MARCH, Memory-Anchor Routing across Context History, which turns the transient trajectory of a recurrent model into a growing bank of addressable states that the model can selectively read back. The architecture solves a specific failure of recurrent models. Self-attention keeps fine-grained access to every prior token but pays a quadratic training cost and a key-value cache that grows with sequence length. Recurrent and linear-attention models compress the prefix into a fixed-size state for constant-memory decoding, but they expose only the latest state for reading, so once an earlier association is attenuated or overwritten, it is gone. MARCH fixes that by periodically checkpointing the evolving recurrent state. At boundaries placed every 512 tokens, the model snapshots its cumulative state into a state anchor and pairs it with a compact routing key. item.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement
item.description: By Yi Ding, Ruqi Zhang (Purdue University) Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement, by Yi Ding and Ruqi Zhang, from the Department of Computer Science at Purdue University. The short version of a long argument: on-policy distillation, one of the most popular token-level post-training recipes of the last year, is not actually distilling. The students get better, but the gains come from suppressing the model's own low-probability tokens, an operation that needs no teacher at all. The authors demonstrate this with controlled ablations, then turn the diagnosis into OPSA, a supervision-free training rule that beats on-policy distillation by 16.77 points on AIME24. To set up the problem: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, like GRPO and DAPO, samples a group of responses per question and normalizes the verifiable rewards within the group to get advantages. The weakness is sparsity. When several responses in a group get the same correctness outcome, their normalized advantages vanish and the learning signal dies. On-policy distillation fixes that with dense supervision: a stronger teacher scores every token of the student's own rollouts, and the per-token advantage is the log-ratio of the teacher's probability over the student's, a reverse KL estimator. The catch is practical: you need shared vocabularies and white-box access to teacher logits. On-policy self-distillation keeps the paradigm but swaps in a hinted version of the policy itself as teacher. The authors argue all of these share the same fatal assumption: that a teacher scoring prefixes it would never generate itself is still giving meaningful supervision.

item.title: PaperGym: Rubric-Centered Evolution for Research-Plan Generation
item.description: By Yuhan Wang, Zhengxi Lu, Yuchen Yan (Zhejiang University) PaperGym: Rubric-Centered Evolution for Research-Plan Generation, by Yuhan Wang, Zhengxi Lu, and Yuchen Yan, from Zhejiang University. The problem it targets: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has no home for research planning, because a research plan has no checkable answer. Math and code generation work with RLVR because every problem ships with an automatic checker. A research plan does not. You cannot diff a proposed experimental design against a golden file, and expert review does not scale to training. So how do you train a model to write good research plans? The scientific literature already contains the raw material at scale: millions of papers, each posing a realistic problem and developing a solution. PaperGym is a framework that converts each paper into a complete training environment, with a question, a reference answer, and a grading rubric, and then trains on it in two stages. The authors release the pipeline, a corpus of 20,000 instances called PaperGym-20k, and two held-out benchmarks. The data construction is the first contribution, and it targets a real flaw in prior rubric-based datasets. Existing pipelines pull the question and the grading criteria from the same part of a paper, so the criteria often restate the question. The authors measured this: in existing datasets, 11.90 to 34.10 percent of criteria can be inferred from the question alone. That means a model can raise its reward by paraphrasing the question back at the judge. PaperGym instead exploits paper structure. It decomposes each paper into four stages, Research Goal, Background, Research Method, and Experimental Design, using a map-reduce extraction with Qwen3-235B-A22B. item.title: CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation
item.description: By Shangqing Tu, Daniel Zhang-Li, Yucheng Wang (CogEvol Inc.; Tsinghua University) CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation, by the CogEvol Team, from CogEvol Inc. and Tsinghua University, with first authors Shangqing Tu, Daniel Zhang-Li, and Yucheng Wang. This is a new foundation-model family, and that matters for this show. CogEvol is a pair of models, a 4B and a 27B, trained specifically for one narrow job: Learning Environment Generation. Given a course brief, it produces a finished learning artifact in a single pass, either structured-JSON slides or a self-contained interactive HTML page. The claim is efficiency and reliability: across 220,000 production requests, a slide completes in a median of 17 seconds and an interactive page in 59, replacing the minutes-long multi-turn agent scaffolding that was the incumbent approach. The 4B is released openly under Apache 2.0; the 27B has served live production traffic in collaboration with the OpenMAIC team since August 2026. I will be precise about one thing up front. CogEvol is built entirely through post-training on top of public base models. The 27B starts from Qwen3.8-27B, a hybrid architecture interleaving 48 gated-delta-net linear-attention layers with 16 full-attention layers and a multi-token-prediction head; the 4B starts from the dense Qwen3.5-4B. The authors contribute everything above the base: the data pipelines, hybrid reward and RL recipes, evaluation suites, and serving infrastructure. So this is a capability release, not a new pre-trained base, and I am flagging it as a foundation-model technical report in the sense the standing rule intends, a new named family of production models for a specific task, not because they trained a transformer from scratch.

item.title: Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation
item.description: By Jiale Kang, Ziyin Yue, Zheng Zhan (Yuanshi Intelligence; Microsoft Research; CUHK) Normalized Low-Rank Adaptation, by Jiale Kang, Ziyin Yue, and Zheng Zhan, from Yuanshi Intelligence, Microsoft Research, and the Chinese University of Hong Kong. The one-line version: normalizing LoRA's down-projection matrix, either continuously or just at initialization, consistently speeds up convergence and improves accuracy across pretraining, finetuning, and reinforcement learning, with no extra parameters or inference cost. LoRA is the default tool for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and the reasons are practical: you train a tiny low-rank pair of matrices instead of the full weights, and the update can be merged back into the base model at deployment. But the training dynamics of that low-rank pair have never really been interrogated. The observation this paper builds on is asymmetric: because LoRA initializes the up-projection to zero, the very first gradients flow almost entirely through the down-projection. Whatever the scale structure of that down-projection is at step zero largely dictates the early trajectory of the whole adapter, and that structure is currently left to random initialization. The fix is a one-line constraint. For a down-projection A with rank dimension r, NoRA normalizes each column of A to unit norm along the rank direction, so every input coordinate is projected through a unit-length latent direction. The key design choice is that this normalization depends on the LoRA parameters, not on the input. That keeps the update linear in the input, which means the normalized adapter can still be absorbed into the pretrained weight matrix after training. You keep the mergeability that makes LoRA deployable, and you only pay a per-step normalization during training.

item.title: SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning
item.description: By Jonghyun Song, Sangjun Song, Minjae Oh (Seoul National University) SHAPE of Chain-of-Thought in Math Reasoning, by Jonghyun Song, Sangjun Song, and Minjae Oh, from the Graduate School of Data Science and the Department of Mathematics Education at Seoul National University. The premise: stop treating a math chain-of-thought as a bag of tokens and start reading it the way a mathematics educator would, tracking which interpretation of the problem the model is working in and which concrete mathematical moves it makes. The framework, called SHAPE, borrows two objects from decades of mathematical problem-solving research. The first is a semantic space, the evolving interpretation under which the model is solving a problem, algebraic, geometric, numerical, and so on. A single correct solution can move between several of these; the model might set up an equation, abandon it to try concrete numbers, then come back to the algebra. The second is a heuristic, the visible mathematical action taken inside a space: simplifying the problem, working backward, introducing an auxiliary object, making cases. These come from Pólya, Schoenfeld, and the think-aloud protocol tradition in mathematics education, where a human solver's verbalizations have been coded into exactly this kind of space-and-move structure for decades. The pipeline is an annotator, they use Grok-4.1-Fast for the labeling, that reads a CoT trace content unit by content unit, tags the heuristic of each unit, and tracks the semantic-space state as it changes, maintaining a memory buffer so it knows when the model is returning to a space it already visited versus opening a new one.

item.title: Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision: A Path toward Superintelligence
item.description: By Zhiqin Yang, Jingwen Fu, Yuhan Liu (HKUST; Zhongguancun Academy; Xi'an Jiaotong University) Scaling Large Reasoning Models beyond Human Supervision, by Zhiqin Yang, Jingwen Fu, and Yuhan Liu, from HKUST, the Zhongguancun Academy, and Xi'an Jiaotong University, with a large corresponding-author team spanning a dozen institutions. The question it organizes around: as large reasoning models keep improving, human supervision is gradually receding from the learning loop, so how does a model keep getting better once the person who wrote the answer, or the rubric, or the environment, is no longer in the room? This is a survey and a position paper, not a new method, and I want to be clear about that from the start. Its value is as a map. It builds a taxonomy that the field has been using inconsistently, and it maintains a continuously updated GitHub repository that tracks the latest systems as they appear. The central organizing device is a five-level ladder, L0 through L4, that classifies where the supervision in a training loop is coming from, and which parts of the loop are still under human control. The ladder is worth stating in full because it is the paper's main contribution. L0 is per-instance human supervision: every training example is paired with a human-provided answer, preference, or judgment that is its target. That is classic supervised learning and the human-in-the-loop reward modeling of early RLHF. L1 is human-grounded evaluation: the human criteria are encoded once into a reusable reward model, rubric, or language-model judge, so the same standard can be applied across many trajectories without a person looking at each one. item.title: DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents
item.description: By Hangrui Xu, Jiarui Wang, Yang Yang (ByteDance; University of Science and Technology of China) DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents, by Hangrui Xu, Jiarui Wang, and Yang Yang of ByteDance, with further authors and Yan Song of the University of Science and Technology of China. The paper attacks a specific, expensive failure in agent training: when a compact student imitates a frontier teacher on multi-turn tool-calling tasks, the standard recipes, full-trajectory supervised fine-tuning and grouped reinforcement learning, both flatten what is actually a graph into a line, and that flattening has a measurable cost. The structural claim first. For tasks with order-independent sub-goals, say fetch three independent facts before writing the answer, many action orders are equally valid, and distinct trajectories routinely diverge and then reconverge at the same intermediate state, because what matters is the information acquired, not the tool syntax that acquired it. The optimal solution space is a combinatorial diamond lattice. Full-trajectory SFT forces every valid ordering to compete against one canonical ordering, so it overwrites valid exploration; the authors call this topological collapse. Grouped reinforcement learning has the mirror-image failure: a terminal reward spread across all tokens penalizes perfectly fine intermediate tool calls inside failed trajectories, credit misassignment. Hindsight methods that relabel failed trajectories still treat the interaction as a linear sequence and cannot tell fatal errors from harmless detours.

item.title: J-ZERO: Unified Challenger-Solver-Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data
item.description: By Gyouk Chu, Myeongho Jeon, Eunho Yang (KAIST) J-ZERO: Unified Challenger-Solver-Judge Co-Evolution from Zero Data, by Gyouk Chu, Myeongho Jeon, and Eunho Yang of KAIST. Zero-data self-play is now a real thing: one model spawns a Challenger that invents tasks and a Solver that learns to answer them, with no external data. It works well where answers can be checked, code execution or majority voting. It stalls everywhere else, because in open-ended domains the learning signal is a reward model, and a frozen judge can only push the solver toward preferences the judge has already internalized. Once the solver saturates the distinctions the judge can make, training produces nothing. The prior fix, G-Zero, kept the judge frozen and worked around it. This paper's move is more direct: let the judge co-evolve inside the loop, and solve the circularity problem, if every signal comes from the same system, what new preference information ever enters, by constructing preference labels from structural asymmetries that hold by construction, independent of any judge scores. The loop has three roles and three phases per iteration. The Challenger generates tasks; its reward is one minus the mean judge score of the solver's attempts on the task, minus a repetition penalty computed by clustering near-duplicate tasks with pairwise BLEU distance, with a format check requiring a well-formed question tag; malformed generations get a negative reward. It is trained with grouped policy optimization to minimize that composite reward, adversarial but deliberately not zero-sum, since the challenger also has diversity and validity constraints. item.title: Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning
item.description: By Yifan Zhang, Steve Ta, Jasper Zhang (ByteDance Seed; Princeton University; Tsinghua University; UCLA; Hyperbolic Labs) Fast Weight Attention for Continual Learning, by Yifan Zhang of ByteDance Seed and Princeton University, Steve Ta and Jasper Zhang, with further authors from ByteDance Seed, Princeton, Tsinghua, UCLA, and Hyperbolic Labs, including Andrew Chi-Chih Yao among the corresponding authors. The framing is worth pausing on, because it reframes an architecture debate as a learning problem. Standard attention externalizes memory as a growing key-value cache: nothing is ever compressed, nothing is ever forgotten, and quadratic cost follows. State-space models and fast-weight architectures instead compress the whole context into a fixed-size recurrent state, which means the state update is literally an online learning rule, a little gradient step executed every token, inside the forward pass. Seen that way, the real design question for these architectures is not what shape the state has but what objective that internal learning rule is actually optimizing, and when it gets to see its training pairs. That question has been implicit in every linear-attention and Delta-network paper so far; this one makes it explicit and finds that the field has been using the wrong pairing. The central observation is a one-position misalignment. Under read-after-write autoregressive semantics, when the model is predicting token t, the state it reads was last written at t minus one; the value that becomes available at step t should therefore be bound to the prefix feature that was available when it was predicted, the key from the previous position, not the key from the current one. Most prior recurrences bind the same-step pair, current key with current value. item.title: Blind Men and the Elephant: Probing the Epistemic Myopia of LLMs under Long-Tail Divergent Knowledge
item.description: By Zhuoshi Pan, Junru Lu, Yan Qian (Tsinghua University; Tencent Youtu Lab; University of Warwick) Blind Men and the Elephant: Probing the Epistemic Myopia of LLMs under Long-Tail Divergent Knowledge, by Zhuoshi Pan of Tsinghua University and Tencent Youtu Lab, Junru Lu and Yan Qian, with further authors from Tsinghua, Tencent Youtu Lab, and the University of Warwick. The benchmark asks a question that standard factual QA cannot ask: not whether a model knows a rare fact, but whether it knows all the credible versions of that fact that its training data contained. The parable in the title is the failure mode: each blind man touches one part of the elephant and generalizes; a model that read one account of a disputed birth date and only ever reproduces that account has the same pathology, and because conventional QA scores a single canonical answer, the pathology is invisible. The evaluation is fully closed-book: no source documents, no retrieval, no tools, just the question, so whatever the model answers comes from parametric memory alone, which is what makes the measurement about what training actually retained rather than about reasoning over evidence. The construction pipeline is the reusable contribution. item.title: Self-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models without Teacher
item.description: By Shiyi Zhang, Mushui Liu, Yunze Tong (Tsinghua University; Zhejiang University; Alibaba Group) Self-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Flow Matching Models without Teacher, by Shiyi Zhang of Tsinghua University and Alibaba Group, Mushui Liu of Zhejiang University and Alibaba Group, and Yunze Tong of Zhejiang University, with further authors from Alibaba Group. The paper targets an expensive habit in generative-model alignment: every time you want to steer a flow-matching image model toward a new objective, the on-policy distillation approach says train a specialized teacher first, then distill from it. Three objectives, three teachers, weeks of GPU time before the student learns anything. Self-OPD removes the teacher entirely and shows the student can generate its own step-wise supervision by exploring around its own trajectory, and the resulting model beats teacher-based distillation on the paper's mixed-objective benchmark. The two prior paradigms frame the problem. Reinforcement-learning approaches like Flow-GRPO treat denoising as a sequential decision process, but the reward arrives only at the end of the full denoising trajectory, so credit must be assigned backward through many steps with high-variance gradients, and mixing several reward models makes multi-objective training fragile because different rewards favor different visual properties. On-policy distillation gives dense, per-step supervision by regressing the student's velocity field toward a pretrained teacher's prediction at every denoising step, which is stable and sample-efficient, but each new objective needs its own teacher, the student is capped by that teacher's quality and bias, and merging multiple teachers at the velocity-field level creates conflicting update directions. Self-OPD keeps the dense per-step structure and replaces the teacher with the student's own local exploration.

The setting is test-time training: a model improves on the very problems it is about to be evaluated on, with no answer key, because labels never arrive. Every strong post-training recipe we have, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards and on-policy self-distillation, assumes an oracle that grades outputs or hands the teacher the right answer. TTPO's contribution is an asymmetric objective that survives a majority-vote pseudo-label being wrong, which on competition math it usually is, and the empirical claim is that this label-free recipe matches the label-supervised version. The problem structure first. Sample a group of rollouts per problem, cluster the final answers by mathematical equivalence, and take the largest cluster as the pseudo-label. On AIME 2026 with the Qwen3 one point seven B base model, that pseudo-label is wrong for about eighty-five percent of prompts. The prior approaches all break on this. TTRL uses the pseudo-label as a reward, so a wrong majority reinforces its own error once per trajectory. The dangerous variant is dense supervision: condition the same model on the pseudo-answer to form a teacher, and distill the student toward it. A corrupted reward misleads once per trajectory; a corrupted teacher misleads at every token.

item.title: Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report
item.description: By TaoLive AIGC LLM Team, Yuhan Sun, Wenhao Lin (Alibaba Group) Training Agents to Evolve with Their Harness: TaoLive Digital Avatar Agent Technical Report, by the TaoLive AIGC LLM team at Alibaba, with Yuhan Sun and Wenhao Lin among the listed authors. The setting is live-stream e-commerce: an AI avatar answers product questions and runs marketing playbooks on air, where every reply is public, the latency budget is seconds, and the business rules change weekly. The engineering dilemma is real and worth stating plainly. Big models adapt to new rules zero-shot but are too slow; in their tests a frontier model's median end-to-end latency exceeded eleven seconds. Compact models meet the latency target but, trained on one fixed configuration, they memorize skill names, tool names, and prompt templates, and then fail exactly when the harness they memorized changes. Fixed-harness supervised fine-tuning costs seven point seven points on IFEval, a general instruction-following benchmark, which is the measurable signature of that overfitting. Their production answer is an evolvable harness with four independently versioned modules: Skills, which are reply rules and strategies; Hooks, which are validation checkpoints that can force retries; a system prompt pipeline; and a tool registry wired to commerce services. Behavior changes ship as harness edits, not retraining. A human-in-the-loop process they call harness evolution diagnoses failures, proposes edits, and evaluates: on a development set of four hundred eighty-two cases annotated by three people, the first evolution round lifted accuracy from eighty-two point four to ninety-two point one but dropped effectiveness to eighty-four point two, the second round reached ninety-two point six and ninety-two point eight and was selected as the engineering stopping point, and further long-tail rules regressed one or both dimensions.

item.description: By Apodex Team (Apodex) FrontierChallenge: Evaluating Scientific Workflow Completion, by the Apodex Team — a benchmark paper with an unusually honest byline: no individual author list at all, just a team name, a leaderboard site, an open evaluation harness on GitHub, and a dataset release. item.description: By Zihao Wu, Hongyao Tang, Yi Ma (Tianjin University; Shanxi University; Imperial College London) WarpSAC: Rethinking Off-Policy Stabilizers for Massively Parallel Reinforcement Learning, by Zihao Wu of Tianjin University, Hongyao Tang of Shanxi University, Yi Ma of Imperial College London, and colleagues including Jianye Hao. item.description: By Zixuan Wang, Yanrui Miao, Yongliang Shen (Zhejiang University; Baidu) Agent-G-squared: Guidance as a Gaussian distribution per task — from Zixuan Wang and Yanrui Miao of Zhejiang University working with Baidu, corresponding author Yongliang Shen. item.title: Gated Recurrent Transformers: Expressive Depth through Recurrent Modulation
item.description: By Amr Hegazy, Amr Alanwar, Mostafa Elhoushi (The German University in Cairo; Technical University of Munich; Cerebras Systems) Gated Recurrent Transformers: Expressive Depth through Recurrent Modulation, by Amr Hegazy of the German University in Cairo, Amr Alanwar of the Technical University of Munich, and Mostafa Elhoushi of Cerebras Systems. The paper starts from a tension every large-model engineer knows: depth and parameters are rigidly coupled in a standard transformer, because every layer carries its own weights, so the memory bill grows exactly as fast as the expressivity. Weight tying breaks that coupling, but naive tying forces an identical transformation onto what are radically different representational stages, and the representation after the first recurrence is nothing like the one after the eighth, so a static shared layer collapses the very functional diversity that makes depth valuable. The paper grounds this in a framing worth repeating: a finite set of states applied iteratively is enough to compute anything computable, so the power of a reasoning system may lie in the depth of iteration rather than the breadth of parameters, and recurrent depth is the hidden-state analogue of test-time chain-of-thought, thinking longer within the residual stream instead of spending tokens. The paper's answer to the collapse problem is borrowed from an old idea: treat the hidden state across recurrences the way a GRU treats its state across time, and let a learned gate decide, element by element, how much of the shared block's output to absorb at each pass. The same weights become fixed in parameters but dynamic in behavior.

item.title: GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture
item.description: By Angen Ye, Axiang Sun, Can Jin (GigaAI) GigaBrain-0.7: Scaling Embodied Foundation Models to Emergent Capabilities with a Three-System Architecture, by Angen Ye, Axiang Sun, and Can Jin — the first three names of a large alphabetically ordered team at GigaAI. The paper describes an embodied foundation model built as three cooperating systems: a vision-language planner, a flow-matching action generator, and a world-model-based predictor that supplies imagined subgoal images and value signals to the controller. The team pretrained it on roughly thirty-seven thousand hours of robot and human manipulation data plus about two hundred seventy-two million vision-language samples, and argues that scale alone starts producing reliable behaviors that small models do not show. The framing question is worth restating because the whole paper hangs on it. Vision-language-action models have become the default recipe for generalist robots, but most systems are trained and evaluated at modest data scale on narrow task suites. The authors ask two things at once: does architectural design still matter once you scale heterogeneous pretraining data, and does real-robot competence improve smoothly or discontinuously as data grows. Their answer is that both hold: architecture choices change what scaling is worth, and several capabilities they care about — deformable-object folding, sustained contact tasks — barely work at small data fractions and become dependable only near full scale.

item.description: By Sungho Park, Wonjoong Kim, Rongyuan Tan (POSTECH; KAIST; SUSTech; Microsoft) AutoSaddler: Automatic Harness Optimization with Durable Updates from Agent Execution Traces, by Sungho Park of POSTECH, Wonjoong Kim of KAIST, and Rongyuan Tan of Southern University of Science and Technology, with colleagues at Microsoft where the first author interned. The premise: language-model agents stay unreliable on long-horizon tasks partly because the scaffolding around the model — prompts, tool definitions, control flow — is hand-tuned folklore. AutoSaddler treats that harness as the thing to train: an offline optimization loop that runs the agent on mini-batches of tasks, diagnoses failed traces against the harness source code, generates targeted patches, keeps what validates, and remembers everything in a search graph. Across three agent benchmarks it lifts pass-at-one by nine to ten percentage points over well-regarded manual harnesses. item.title: SecOPD: Mitigating Adaptive Prompt Injections by On-Policy Distillation
item.description: By Yibo Peng, Long Lian, David Wagner (UC Berkeley) SecOPD: Mitigating Adaptive Prompt Injections by On-Policy Distillation, by Yibo Peng, Long Lian, David Wagner, and Sizhe Chen at the University of California, Berkeley, with Wagner and Chen jointly supervising. A trusted user instruction sits in one message; untrusted external data — web pages, documents, tool outputs — sits in another, using a dedicated input message type added to the chat template. The adversary controls only the untrusted field and may embed any instruction there. The defended model should keep using external data as context while never obeying instructions inside it. This is indirect injection where the user is benign; the authors state plainly that jailbreaks, direct injections, and malicious-user attacks are out of scope. They also assume the system already knows which input parts are trusted, which sidesteps a hard open problem rather than solving it. item.title: CyberFactory: Scaling Cyber Security Capabilities with Instances from the Wild
item.description: By Jian Yang, Haau-Sing Li, Shawn Guo (Beihang University; ELLIS; IQuest Research; Singapore Management University) CyberFactory: Scaling Cyber Security Capabilities with Instances from the Wild, by Jian Yang of Beihang University, Haau-Sing Li of ELLIS, and Shawn Guo of IQuest Research, with collaborators including a corresponding author at Singapore Management University. The paper's pitch is a full recipe rather than just weights: an open-source framework that converts public vulnerability records into executable, verifiable training tasks spanning proof-of-concept generation, vulnerability patching, and security question answering, then trains a model called OpenAegis on agentic trajectories grounded in those tasks. On the CyberGym reproduction benchmark under a one-hour-per-task budget, OpenAegis reaches fifty-eight point one percent pass-at-one — twenty-eight and a half points above its own Qwen 3.5 base checkpoint at the same size, and ahead of substantially larger frontier models evaluated under identical scaffolding. The evaluation target deserves explanation first because everything else serves it. A task asks the agent to produce a proof-of-concept input that reproduces a real vulnerability, given only a natural-language description and the codebase. Success is judged by a differential oracle: the input must trigger the sanitizer failure on the pre-patch build and leave the patched build unharmed. That two-sided check rules out inputs that crash for incidental reasons and makes success machine-checkable — no human grader, no string matching against an expected answer. item.description: By Zhaochen Yu, Yingcheng Wu, Zhenfei Yin (NUS; Stanford University; University of Oxford; Princeton University) Recursive Experiential–Working Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agent Harnesses, by Zhaochen Yu of the National University of Singapore, Yingcheng Wu of Stanford University, and Zhenfei Yin of the University of Oxford, with senior authors at Princeton University. Instead an external memory-control layer — skills, working-state schema, invocation policy, verification checks — evolves through a validation-gated loop while everything else stays frozen. Across four long-horizon benchmarks and ten models, that layer improves task success in thirty-five of thirty-seven completed pairings, including lifting Claude Opus five from seventy-two point four to eighty-seven point nine percent on a retail tool-use benchmark. The two design moves deserve separate treatment because they carry separate lessons. First, how memory gets used during a task. Prior experiential-memory harnesses retrieve skills against either the initial instruction or the entire chat history, and both degrade as execution unfolds — instructions go stale, histories fill with completed steps and noise. Recuris maintains instead a compact structured working state where each goal records content, status — pending, done, or blocked — supporting evidence, and any blocker. item.title: Apodex 1.1: Scaling Agentic Intelligence for Complex Work
item.description: By Apodex Team, B. An, B. Li (Apodex) Apodex 1.1: Scaling Agentic Intelligence for Complex Work, by the 71-author Apodex Team, with B. An, B. Li, and colleagues at Apodex, a company that publishes model weights on Hugging Face and runs an API platform alongside its research reports. The technical report frames one capability as the actual target: working capability, defined as sustained, verifiable progress toward a real-world objective. The argument is that general-purpose models reason and summarize adequately, but complex professional work requires sustained interaction with files, information sources, and executable code, plus state maintenance across failures and delivery of artifacts that survive checking. The paper scales that capability along two declared axes, Environment Scaling and Agentic Coordination Scaling, and reports results across professional work, finance, science, mathematics, search, and coding. Prior agentic systems mostly optimize isolated responses or single-domain loops. ReAct established the reasoning, action, observation cycle; SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench grade repository and command-line work; APEX-Agents grades long-horizon cross-application tasks designed by investment bankers, consultants, and lawyers; deep-research systems handle open-ended information seeking. What is missing in most of that line of work is a single model and runtime where file, search, and code execution compose inside one policy, with coordination treated as a trained behavior rather than a prompted wrapper. Apodex 1.0 was this group's earlier verification-centric agent team. Version 1.1 keeps the architecture and changes three things materially: broader verifiable training environments, an explicit external task board with asynchronous human intervention, and a dedicated synthesis stage separated from team execution.

item.title: TLive-Omni: An Omni-Modal Understanding Model for E-Commerce Live Streaming
item.description: By Yibo Hu; Yu Qian; Mao Gu; Yingfan Tao (Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba) **Cold open:** Picture a livestream that never stops. A host talks for six straight hours about a moisturizer, holds it up to the camera, peels off the label so you can read the ingredients, while hundreds of viewers type questions faster than any human moderator could answer. When does the discount code appear? Does it work on sensitive skin? What did the price look like half an hour ago? Every fact a viewer needs lives somewhere in that torrent of speech, pixels, and scrolling text — and no single modality carries it alone. Taming that torrent is the goal of TLive-Omni, a new system from Yibo Hu, Yu Qian, Mao Gu, Yingfan Tao, and their colleagues at Taobao & Tmall Group of Alibaba. The paper — TLive-Omni: An Omni-Modal Understanding Model for E-Commerce Live Streaming — appeared on arXiv on August twenty-first, twenty twenty-six, under the plain byline TLive-Omni Team. With it came two open checkpoints, at four billion and nine billion parameters, published on Hugging Face and GitHub. Here is what they built, how they trained it, and where the numbers genuinely stand. Under the hood this is a text-output omni model: a Qwen3.5 vision-language backbone, extended with the audio transformer encoder from Qwen3-Omni, grafted into the same embedding space through a lightweight two-layer aligner. That audio encoder was pretrained from scratch on twenty million hours of audio and compresses speech to roughly thirteen tokens per second, which is what makes long recordings affordable. The whole system accepts up to two hundred fifty-six thousand multimodal tokens of context — hours of stream in a single pass.

item.title: MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks
item.description: By Yi Zhu, Xiongwei Wu, Qiyi Wang (MAI Team, Alibaba Token Foundry) MobilePA-Bench: Benchmarking Mobile Planner Agents on Complex Real-World Tasks, by Yi Zhu, Xiongwei Wu, and Qiyi Wang of the MAI Team at Alibaba Token Foundry. The premise is narrow and worth stating precisely. As phone assistants mature into agents that place calls, book travel, and restructure device settings on a user's behalf, there has been no agreed instrument for measuring whether a planner actually finishes such jobs. This paper builds one and reports what happens when thirteen frontier models are pushed through it. Existing benchmarks split into two camps, and the authors document blind spots in both. GUI-centric suites — AndroidWorld, OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, MobiBench — put a vision-language model in front of screenshots and grade pixel-level navigation. That exercises perception, but tapping icons is a fraction of what a competent phone agent does, and rendering-heavy environments carry latencies that make them impractical for reinforcement learning rollouts. Static function-calling suites — the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, ToolBench, DroidCall, AppBench — sit at the opposite extreme: the model emits a JSON blob and an answer key grades the string, offline, with no live state. Nothing executes, so runtime exceptions, permission boundaries, and call dependencies never enter the picture. item.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
item.description: By Seth Karten, Alex L. Zhang, Kevin Thomas (Princeton University; Prime Intellect; MIT) Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness, by Seth Karten of Princeton University and Prime Intellect, Alex L. Zhang of Prime Intellect and MIT, and Kevin Thomas of Prime Intellect, together with additional co-authors from those groups. The paper presents an open-source agent harness built around a persistent IPython execution layer, recursive language-model subagents, direct agent-to-agent messaging, and a versioned store of prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications, and reports evaluations spanning interactive reasoning, long-context coding, GPU kernel generation, emulator construction, and multi-day autonomous runs. The framing: a language model is a bounded sequential processor whose next decision conditions only on fixed weights and whatever sits in the active context. A harness supplies everything else. The authors organize the resulting state into four levels: model weights as level zero, active context as level one, a persistent REPL plus recursive subagents as level two, and disk-backed history, artifacts, memories, skills, prompts, and subagent specifications as level three. Their measurement argument is the motivating claim. A model should fail an evaluation because the task exceeds its capability, not because the harness dropped state, restricted useful actions, miscounted resources, or terminated prematurely. The components existed separately before. Recursive Language Models made context handling programmable; Continual Harness made prompts and skills revisable from trajectory history. What was missing was one substrate integrating both with persistence, recovery, verification, and unified accounting, and that integration is the contribution here.

item.description: By Yongqi Tong, Tan Li Hui Faith, Choy Zhen Wen Marcus (Ant International) ARC: Fair Relative Advantage Comparison in Open-Ended Real-World Interaction, by Yongqi Tong, Tan Li Hui Faith, and Choy Zhen Wen Marcus, equal-contribution first authors at Ant International, with Zhou Jin, Kewei Fu, Jiang-Ming Yang, Jianshe Li, and Xin Zhang as coauthors. The paper addresses a specific failure mode in group-based reinforcement learning for agents: when one rollout group mixes different conversation strategies, relative advantages stop measuring response quality and start measuring whatever interaction style the reward model happens to prefer. First the problem, because the mechanism only makes sense against it. Group-based methods such as GRPO sample several responses per prompt, subtract the group mean reward, and use the centered value as the advantage. That signal is interpretable only when the compared rollouts are behaviorally comparable. In open-ended interaction they often are not: for the same dialogue state the agent may answer directly from memory, ask for clarification first, stream progress updates while tools run, or restate intent and confirm before an irreversible action. All of these can be task-appropriate. Reward models carry exposure, length, and style bias, so when a group spans qualitatively different behaviors, the centered reward absorbs region-specific reward preference along with genuine quality differences. The authors formalize this as a fairness property: a reward model is delta-fair if two equally good responses following different strategies score within delta of each other, and they argue real reward models violate it systematically in agent settings where interaction appropriateness lacks ground truth. item.title: EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning
item.description: By Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, Rujun Han (Washington University in St. Louis; Google Cloud AI Research; Google Cloud; University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill) EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning, by Chengsong Huang, Zifeng Wang, and Rujun Han, with fourteen more authors including Burak Gokturk, Tomas Pfister, and Chen-Yu Lee. Huang did this work while interning at Google Cloud AI Research, and the affiliation list covers Washington University in St. Louis, Google Cloud AI Research, Google Cloud, and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Here is the premise, and it is a reasonable one. As language models become agents, the scarce resource for training shifts from curated text data to interactive environments. Those environments are hand-built: someone hardcodes interaction logic and a verifier, and the result behaves identically whether it faces a novice or a competent policy. Two failure modes follow. A static environment cannot target the specific weaknesses of the policy you actually have, and once the policy learns to solve its existing tasks, the environment has nothing left to teach. Automated environment generation exists as an alternative, with systems like GenEnv simulating environments and their feedback inside a model, VeriEnv synthesizing executable environments programmatically, and SWE-smith generating new task instances within an existing benchmark. But those pipelines are domain-specific, each built separately for web navigation, programming, or tool use, and because both tasks and verifiers come out of a model, teams over-generate and filter heavily without ever guaranteeing correctness. EnvHarness takes a different position: stop authoring new environments, and reshape the ones you already trust.

item.title: FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis
item.description: By Kou Shi, Zun Wang, Qisheng Su (MoE Key Lab of BIPC, University of Science and Technology of China; Shanghai AI Laboratory; Fudan University) FACET: Preserving Source Intent and Executable State in Terminal Task Synthesis, by Kou Shi, Zun Wang, and Qisheng Su, with ten more authors including Feng Zhao as corresponding author. The affiliations are the MoE Key Lab of BIPC at the University of Science and Technology of China, Shanghai AI Laboratory, and Fudan University. The problem this paper attacks is concrete: training terminal agents needs scalable, executable supervision, and every synthesized terminal task is a tightly coupled bundle of an instruction, an initialized environment, a reference solution, and an executable verifier, packaged in the Harbor format that Terminal-Bench uses. If those artifacts are generated under inconsistent assumptions you get tasks that cannot be solved or that grade incorrectly. Two failure mechanisms dominate multi-stage synthesis pipelines. First, information loss: source material rich in capabilities, dependencies, intermediate states, input-output contracts, and procedural constraints gets progressively compressed into a simplified task description, preserving only a fraction of the available structure. Second, artifact drift: an instruction references a file never realized in the environment, a solution assumes a different schema or dependency version, or a verifier tests a state the generated task cannot produce. Passing textual specifications between generation stages mitigates neither problem, because text is not a shared realized state.

item.description: By Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, Yining Zheng (Shanghai Innovation Institute; Fudan University) SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?, by Zhipeng Xu, Jiahao Lu, and Yining Zheng, with Yuxin Wang and Xipeng Qiu as corresponding authors, all affiliated with the Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University. item.title: Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation
item.description: By Silin Chen, Haoyi Teng, Xiaodong Gu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Chongqing University) Repo0: Design-Driven Zero-to-All Code Generation, by Silin Chen and Haoyi Teng as equal first authors, Xiaodong Gu as corresponding author, with Yuling Shi, Jiale Huang, Yongpan Wang, Hongyu Zhang, and Haibing Guan. The setting is zero-to-all code generation: an agent receives natural-language requirements and must construct an entire software project from nothing while maintaining a modular repository architecture throughout. Most existing systems quietly assume the opposite, that component boundaries, package organization, and dependency graphs are already given, which is why repository-completion work looks so much better than it should. The authors' diagnosis of prior systems, including RPG, the strongest graph-based baseline, is that they treat software design as a static artifact: a perfect architectural blueprint generated in one initial planning stage, then rigidly executed. Anyone who has shipped software knows the blueprint is wrong by the time implementation starts; generated code reveals whether planned components were ever cohesive or whether dependency edges are entangled. Repo0's answer is continuous structural evolution around an explicit architectural state, instantiated as what they call a Dual-DAG. Two directed acyclic graphs plus an alignment relation. The requirement-level DAG holds high-level requirements decomposed into sub-requirements, and its edges encode functional coordination: two requirements logically used together and needing joint consideration for behavior, inputs, and outputs. item.title: FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving
item.description: By Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, Zhiying Wu (MAIS and NLPR, CASIA; UCAS; WeChat, Tencent) FlashPrefill V2: Block-Sparse Prefill Attention for Long-Context LLM Serving, by Qihang Fan, Huaibo Huang, and Zhiying Wu, with Bingning Wang as project leader and Ran He. The affiliations are the Institute of Automation of the Chinese Academy of Sciences through its MAIS and NLPR labs, the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, and WeChat at Tencent; the first author completed the work during an internship at WeChat. Context for the audience: attention cost during prefill grows with the square of sequence length, and every training-free sparse-attention method lives or dies on three practical questions. Does accuracy survive aggressive sparsity? Is the kernel competitive with current dense implementations rather than last generation's? And does it work inside a real serving stack with paged KV cache and continuous batching? Their previous FlashPrefill answered none of those fully. It discovered patterns instantaneously using mean-pooled keys and max-based dynamic thresholding, avoiding the global sorting that Top-k selection requires, but accuracy degraded without bound under extreme sparsity, the kernel was built on FlashAttention-2's execution model, which leaves Hopper tensor-core throughput on the table, and it assumed a contiguous KV layout incompatible with any modern serving framework. V2 addresses exactly these three gaps.

item.title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills
item.description: By Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, Ran Li (Southeast University; Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills, by Zeyu Ren, Ling Yue, and Ran Li, with Yishu Wang, Shengxiang Xu, Hanmo Liu, Shaowu Pan, and Shimin Di. The affiliations are Southeast University, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. The gap this paper identifies is real and worth articulating precisely. Workflow-based agents construct procedures at inference time: decomposition, tool calls, code generation, checking, repair. But whatever structure a successful episode discovers gets discarded when the episode ends. Skill libraries preserve reusable routines as executable objects, yet they are typically assembled offline for a fixed task distribution rather than growing from the agent's own problem solving. Text memories such as Agent Workflow Memory sit in between: they describe what worked but cannot be invoked or validated, so reuse still depends on the model re-deriving the procedure from prose. FlowEvo is a training-free framework that closes this loop: successful workflows are compiled into callable skill records stored in a persistent bank, and those skills feed back into later workflow construction either through direct execution or as structured context. Model weights never change.

item.title: Zetta ζ: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence
item.description: By Xin Ding, Liang Mi, Mingzhe Huang (Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University; Z-Trans AI) The paper is "Zetta Zeta: An Efficient Closed-Loop Embodied Harness for Self-Evolving Physical Intelligence." Yes, the Greek letter zeta is genuinely in the title. The first three authors are Xin Ding, Liang Mi, and Mingzhe Huang, leading a fourteen-person list from the Institute for AI Industry Research at Tsinghua University — AIR for short — together with Z-Trans AI. It sits at the top of the day's daily list with 145 upvotes, so a lot of people want this story to be true. Whether it holds up is a fair question, and we will get there. The problem is familiar to anyone who has shipped a robot policy. Vision-language-action models keep failing once they leave the curated evaluation suite, because the things that made training work — dense supervision, verifiable rewards, clean resets — stop existing at deployment time. The usual response is to freeze everything at ship date and route observed failures back to the vendor for the next release cycle, which means every fix waits months and every regression risks undoing old ones. The authors argue the mistake is treating the whole stack as one frozen object. Their split is cleaner: the base policy stays frozen, and the harness around it — runtime critics, recovery routines, rollout plumbing — becomes the part that evolves, using nothing but the stream of episodes the robot already produces during ordinary operation. No new labels, no human-in-the-loop repair queue, no fine-tuning runs that could destabilize the skills the policy already has.

item.title: SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation
item.description: By Yanlun Tu, Huacan Wang, Ziyue Zhou (Midea AIRC; KUKA; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Zhejiang University) The paper is "SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation." item.title: Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL
item.description: By Yunhao Yang, Yuexin Bian, Yunjie Tian (Johns Hopkins University; UC San Diego; University of Exeter) The paper is "Co-RL: Unsupervised Reasoning Emerges from Diverse Cohort in Multi-agent RL." The first three authors are Yunhao Yang, Yuexin Bian, and Yunjie Tian, leading a nine-author group spread across Johns Hopkins University, UC San Diego, and the University of Exeter, with a couple of independent researchers mixed in. At 92 upvotes it sits third on the day, and its promise is the one everybody wants: reasoning improvements from reinforcement learning with zero ground-truth labels. To see the problem, start from the standard recipe. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains models on problems with checkable answers — math with known solutions, code with known outputs — and it works embarrassingly well. The catch is that verifiable answers require humans to have produced them, and as capabilities advance past what people can reliably evaluate, the supervision supply line thins exactly where you want to push. Self-rewarding methods respond by letting the model grade its own completions, no labels needed. The trouble, documented repeatedly, is what happens when a student grades its own exam: the model drifts toward confidently rewarding its own errors, and training collapses into elaborate self-flattery. The most-cited cautionary example is TTRL, which leans on majority voting over the model's own samples — workable early, but as training progresses the votes simply ratify whatever the model already believes, so the pseudo-labels freeze around the model's initial competence instead of stretching it. Every label-free scheme has to answer the same uncomfortable question: where does genuinely new corrective signal enter the system? If the only source of judgment is the model being judged, the honest answer is nowhere.

item.title: OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist
item.description: By Bobo Li, Hao Fei, Tianjie Ju, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu (National University of Singapore; University of Oxford) Hello everyone, and welcome back. The authors argue that everything currently calling itself an AI scientist shares a specific blind spot, and that blind spot is where the actual science lives. To see the argument, look at what existing systems actually consume. Automated research frameworks have gotten genuinely impressive at orchestrating workflows: generate hypotheses, plan experiments, execute code, draft manuscripts. But inspect the input side and you find text, code, class labels, or precomputed summaries — someone else already did the looking, the summarizing, and crucially the deciding about what mattered. The spatial relation between two regions of a tissue slide, the temporal drift across hours of a sensor trace, the cross-channel coupling in a multivariate signal, the procedural detail of how an experiment was physically performed: these are scientifically decisive, and they are exactly what never survives conversion into a scalar feature or a caption. item.title: Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis
item.description: By Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Maksim Kuznetsov, Mathieu Reymond, Vladimir Aladinskiy, Alex Aliper, Alex Zhavoronkov (Insilico Medicine — Abu Dhabi, Montreal, and Hong Kong) Welcome back, everyone. Today's paper is "Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis," by Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Maksim Kuznetsov, Mathieu Reymond, Vladimir Aladinskiy, Alex Aliper, and Alex Zhavoronkov of Insilico Medicine, with labs spanning Abu Dhabi, Montreal, and Hong Kong. It carries thirty-three upvotes on today's board, and underneath the chemistry it is making a methodological argument the broader ML community should hear: some problems are intrinsically one-to-many, and forcing them into single-answer evaluation quietly breaks both your training signal and your benchmarks. Here is the setup. Retrosynthesis asks the question a chemist faces when staring at a target molecule: what known reaction could produce this? It is the core step of computer-aided synthesis planning, and drug discovery lives or dies on synthetic accessibility — designing a compound nobody can manufacture is designing nothing. The structural difficulty is that the answer is rarely unique: a target molecule typically admits many valid precursor sets through many different reaction types, all chemically plausible, several industrially sensible. Single-answer protocols — predict the one right disconnection, score against one ground truth — punish diversity and reward memorizing the majority route. The authors' response is Top-K prompting, used consistently at both training and inference: the model learns to emit a ranked set of plausible disconnections rather than a lone guess, which matches the task's actual geometry instead of fighting it. item.title: Training Leaves Traces: Centered Residual Signatures for Language Model Lineage Verification
item.description: By Aman Singh Thakur, Rayan Khoury (Amazon; Massachusetts Institute of Technology) Welcome back. Today's paper is "Training Leaves Traces: Centered Residual Signatures for Language Model Lineage Verification," by Aman Singh Thakur of Amazon and Rayan Khoury of MIT, sitting with eighteen upvotes on today's board — modest numbers for what might be the most quietly consequential question of the day: given two open-weight model checkpoints, can you tell from the weights alone whether one descends from the other? No training logs, no data, no behavioral testing, no metadata to trust or distrust. Just the tensors. The motivation comes from how model distribution actually works now. Open-weight models move through supply chains rather than as single releases: a base checkpoint gets fine-tuned, quantized, pruned, adapted with low-rank updates, merged with other models, renamed, and redistributed — sometimes documented, often not, and occasionally deliberately obscured. The existing verification toolbox is embarrassingly thin. Cryptographic hashes break the moment any weight changes, which means every legitimate fine-tune invalidates the hash. Metadata and licensing files require honesty from whoever relabeled the model, which is exactly the resource an adversary controls. Behavioral fingerprints — probing outputs to guess ancestry — are confounded by distillation: two models that behave alike need not share a single weight, and two models sharing every weight can be made to behave differently. The paper's framing is precise about what is being claimed: data-free, white-box lineage verification, asking whether ancestry leaves a structural trace in weights themselves that survives benign modification and cannot be removed without breaking the model.

item.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't
item.description: By Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, Hanwen Xing (Princeton University; UC San Diego; Stanford University; University of Southern California; Johns Hopkins University) Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't. First authors Zhiyuan Jiang, Fangrui Huang, and Hanwen Xing, working across Princeton University, UC San Diego, Stanford University, the University of Southern California, and Johns Hopkins University. The paper asks a question most skill evaluations skip entirely: when do agent skills actually help, why do they work, and where do they fail. If you maintain SKILL.md-style packages in production agents, this is a measurement paper worth your attention. Here is the gap being addressed. Skills are structured knowledge packages injected into an agent's environment at inference time. Existing evaluations report aggregate task success with and without skills, which tells you nothing about mechanism. A skill could win because it injects missing facts, because it stabilizes execution, or by accident. Those three explanations imply very different engineering investments, and aggregate success rates cannot distinguish them. The study design is the strongest part of the paper. The authors compare three conditions built from identical source material: Raw, meaning no prior experience; Workflow Memory, meaning cleaned execution traces from prior runs handed to the agent directly; and Skill, meaning a standardized SKILL.md document distilled from exactly the same traces. Because Workflow Memory and Skill are constructed from the same underlying trajectories, any difference between them isolates the effect of representation rather than the effect of having seen past experience. item.title: FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution
item.description: By Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, Melissa Pan (UC Berkeley; University of Texas at Austin; MIT; University of Michigan) FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution. Shuo Yang, Xiaoze Fan, and Melissa Pan led the work, with the author group spanning UC Berkeley, the University of Texas at Austin, MIT, and the University of Michigan—the PDF's first page lists correspondence through Berkeley and UT Austin addresses. The claim: a serving stack co-designed for consumer hardware can run frontier-scale mixture-of-experts models interactively on machines people already own. Skeptical? So was I. The numbers are specific enough to check. The problem first. Open-weight frontier models like GLM-5.2 at 753 billion parameters and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284 billion parameters with 13 billion active per token are free to download and expensive to run. They assume datacenter GPUs whose clusters cost millions of dollars, and hosted APIs remain burdensome for individuals as agentic applications multiply inference demand. Meanwhile over one hundred million consumer machines have discrete GPUs—Steam alone reports more than 200 million monthly active users with discrete NVIDIA GPUs on roughly 72 percent of surveyed systems. Mixture-of-experts architectures make edge serving plausible because each token activates a small subset of experts—DeepSeek-V4-Flash routes to 6 of 256 experts in each of its 43 layers—but existing engines waste that sparsity in three distinct ways.

item.title: ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence
item.description: By Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, Binyu Li (Tsinghua University; University of Michigan; MIT; Harvard University) ASI-Bench: At the Dawn of Artificial Superintelligence. Core authors Junwei Zhou, Zhen Sun, and Binyu Li, from a large collaboration spanning Tsinghua University, the University of Michigan, MIT, Harvard University, Carnegie Mellon University, and several other institutions. The title oversells it; the benchmark does not. What this paper actually delivers is a controlled measurement of how fast frontier agents fall apart when you withdraw human methodological guidance, and that measurement is worth your time. The premise: today's AI mostly learns, compresses, and applies existing human knowledge. Benchmarks test whether systems produce correct answers from learned knowledge or complete tasks under heavy human specification. Nobody jointly measures innovative exploration—choosing how to attack an open research problem—and autonomous scientific execution across general domains, within one project, with guidance progressively removed. Existing options each cover a slice: Humanity's Last Exam is academic question answering; Terminal-Bench is terminal tasks; ScienceAgentBench is scientific analysis under largely fixed workflows; PaperBench is research replication; MLE-Bench is machine-learning engineering; RE-Bench is AI R&D; DiscoveryBench and SciCode cover data-driven discovery and scientific coding. All provide a fixed task specification. None asks whether the agent could have constructed the workflow itself, none spans general scientific domains at project level, and none varies guidance within the same research problem—so a high score can mean genuine discovery or faithful procedure-following, and the two are indistinguishable in the aggregate.

item.title: Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation
item.description: By Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, Xuanyu Liu (Zhejiang University; Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center) Embodied-Navigator: Point, Think, Memorize, and Align for Efficient Navigation. First authors Hongyan Feng, Sunlai Chen, and Xuanyu Liu, from the OmniAl Group of the ACES Lab at Zhejiang University together with the Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center. The system is called TAMP-Nav: Point, Think, Memorize, Align. It reports 66.2 percent success on R2R-CE validation-unseen with a tenth of the training trajectories of some competitors, and it runs inference in about half the time per task. Those efficiency numbers are the real story here. Three bottlenecks motivate the design. First, the geometric gap: vision-language models are pretrained on 2D image-text pairs, but vision-and-language navigation forces them to emit low-level atomic actions like turn left thirty degrees or to regress 3D coordinates, which demands implicit geometric transformations they were never trained to perform and produces spatial hallucinations with poor sample efficiency. Second, the reasoning-efficiency dilemma: chain-of-thought improves high-level planning but existing models trigger it at every step or at fixed intervals, multiplying inference latency for marginal gains. Third, memory: keeping full visual history causes attention dilution and overflow, while discarding history or decaying it loses critical information, and most architectures carry no explicit spatio-temporal coordinates organizing what they keep.

item.title: AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning
item.description: By Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, Haozhe Wang (Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba; ShanghaiTech University; Hong Kong University of Science and Technology) AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning. First authors Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, and Haozhe Wang, from the Qwen Business Unit of Alibaba, ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Institute of Computing Technology, and Southeast University. The problem: video creation agents cannot learn filmmaking from finished films, because a rendered video is not an operable record of the decisions that produced it—scripts, characters, shots, camera language, pacing, and audio design are coupled across space and time in ways the finished pixels do not expose. The proposal is to turn films into structured knowledge graphs that agents can read, query, edit, and reconstruct from—and to use reconstruction error itself as the training signal. The task formulation is an agentic auto-encoder. Three parts. An Agentic Video Encoder governed by a policy implemented as three distinct system prompts covering film-level, shot-level, and keyframe-level understanding, with inter-level context injection propagating information across granularities. A bottleneck that is not a neural embedding but a Film Knowledge Graph. And a fixed decoder: a static rendering pipeline calling frozen generation models as tools, taking reference keyframes and shot-prompt descriptions from the graph and rendering shots sequentially. Because the decoder never changes, any difference in reconstruction quality measures the representation. That is the entire evaluation philosophy—reconstruction fidelity as a proxy for representation faithfulness.

item.title: Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL
item.description: By Zhiyuan He, Siwei Zhang, Zhiwen Zhou (Microsoft; Fudan University; Zhejiang University; University of Edinburgh) Agent Lightning v1.0: Towards Harnessed Agentic RL. First authors Zhiyuan He, Siwei Zhang, and Zhiwen Zhou, from Microsoft, Fudan University, Zhejiang University, and the University of Edinburgh. This paper does two things: it names and systematically characterizes a failure-prone regime—reinforcement learning on agents that run inside their own deployment harnesses—and it ships a roughly 3,500-line framework fixing the identified problems, with a coding-agent result that deserves scrutiny: Qwen3.5-9B improving on SWE-bench Verified from 41.8 to 56.4 percent using reinforcement learning alone on about 6,000 examples. Terminology first. Traditional agentic RL puts the environment loop inside the trainer: prompt tokens, action tokens, observation tokens concatenate into one Markov chain—prompt at step t equals the previous prompt plus the previous action plus the tokenized observation—one training sample per rollout. Harnessed agentic RL means the deploy-time harness—mini-SWE-agent, OpenHands, OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Hermes—owns context construction, tool execution, and control flow, while the training engine observes only LLM request-response pairs crossing an API boundary. Both regimes fit partially observable Markov decision processes, but the latent state now includes harness state, and the policy sees separately constructed prompts per call. The proxy-based disaggregation came from the original Agent Lightning; verl Uni-Agent, AReaL 2.0, slime v0.3.0, and Polar have since adopted it. The contribution here is showing that this paradigm silently breaks four assumptions every standard trainer makes.

item.title: StateM: Reaching 95.3% Raw Accuracy, or a $15 Frontier Run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via Harness Scaling
item.description: By Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, Zhangyang Atlas Wang (Somewhere on the Earth) StateM: Reaching 95.3 percent raw accuracy, or a $15 frontier run, on Terminal-Bench 2.1 via harness scaling. That is arXiv 2608.15089, from Ziheng Qin, Yaxin Lu, and Zhangyang Atlas Wang, joined by Kai Wang, who list their affiliation on the paper's first page as, literally, "Somewhere on the Earth." The work was done in the authors' personal time. The claim deserves attention anyway: without changing a single model weight, their agent runtime lifts GPT-5.5 xhigh from an 83.1 percent reference to 92.1 percent on Terminal-Bench 2.1, and reaches 95.3 percent raw accuracy with GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh across 445 public-submission trials. Let me walk through what the system actually does, what the evidence does and does not cover, and where you should verify before adopting any of it. The premise is familiar to anyone who has babysat a long agent run: the underlying model clearly knows how to do each step, and the run still fails. The agent drifts off-plan, loses track of mutable task state, skips a required check, repeats an unproductive action, or stops before the deliverable is verifiably complete. Benchmarks score the completed job, not the fraction of steps the model understood. The paper frames the dominant alternative responses — more pretraining, more post-training data, longer reasoning, more agents — as orthogonal to its question: how much apparent model failure is actually failure of the surrounding harness, the layer that maintains state, constrains execution, verifies progress, and recovers from errors? item.title: Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization
item.description: By Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, Haichao Zhang (University of Florida; UC San Diego; Northeastern University; Northwestern University; Stanford University; Zillion Network; Universität Innsbruck) The paper is called Learn What's Left, Not What's Mastered: Saturation Aware Advantage Reweighting for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization. The first three authors are Yixuan Wang, Yifei Chen, and Haichao Zhang, working with a nine-person roster that spans the University of Florida, UC San Diego, Northeastern University, Northwestern University, Stanford University together with Zillion Network, and the University of Innsbruck. The arXiv id is 2608.16072, dated August 18, 2026. Here is the problem they take on, and it is one of those problems that is obvious once stated. Group-relative policy optimization is now the de facto standard for post-training language model reasoners. You sample a group of rollouts per prompt, score them, subtract the group mean, divide by the group standard deviation, and push probabilities accordingly. It works because the baseline comes free from the group. The friction starts when you optimize several reward objectives at once — answer correctness, format compliance, a length penalty, a tool-use check, whatever your mixture happens to be. The universal practice is scalarization: sum the components into one reward, then run the usual group normalization on the total. That sum is where signal leaks out. Consider an objective the model has essentially mastered: every rollout in the group earns nearly the same score on it. Its within-group z-score is then pure sampling noise — tiny, directionless, occasionally nonzero for no reason at all. After scalarization, that noise still participates in the total advantage.
