item.title: HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds
item.description: By Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, Jun Gao, et al. (MirroS Lab) Here is a question the world-model community has mostly been avoiding: how do you trust a score that comes with no explanation? Today's paper is HarnessEval-W: Agentifying the Evaluation of Visual Worlds — first authors Weiliang Chen, Haowen Sun, and Jun Gao, joined by co-authors including Jialong Wu, Jiangran Lyu, and Fangfu Liu in a forty-four-author collaboration whose benchmark and tooling ship publicly under the MirroS Lab organization. Their diagnosis is blunt. Current world-model evaluation compresses every prediction into metrics computed brute-force — pixel distances and classifier scores with no reasoning chain anyone can inspect. When two video-world models disagree about whether a cup stays on the table after a robot arm sweeps past, you receive two numbers and zero arguments. This paper's bet is that the evaluator itself should be an agent: something that investigates a generated rollout the way a careful reviewer investigates a manuscript, and leaves behind an evidence trail you can audit line by line. World models are becoming the planning core of embodied systems. An agent imagines forward — if I grasp here, the scene evolves there — and acts on the imagination. As these generators improve, the bottleneck moves from making predictions to grading them, and grading is where the field quietly cut corners. The standard toolkit measures observation overlap frame by frame, plus learned classifiers for physics plausibility. Those scores hide three distinct failure modes inside one average: did the model see what changed, did it predict the right dynamics, and did it remember the object three seconds later? item.title: UI-Mate: A Self-Evolving Companion for Computer-Use Agents
item.description: By Zihan Ding, Longxu Dou, Qi Gao, et al. (Tencent Hy Frontier Team) Today's paper is "UI-Mate: A Self-Evolving Companion for Computer-Use Agents," by Zihan Ding, Longxu Dou, Qi Gao, and twenty-six colleagues spanning Tencent's Hy Frontier team — twenty-nine authors in all. The pitch matches the name: rather than train yet another larger computer-use model, they built a companion that rides along with one, watches it operate, steps in the moment it stalls, and remembers every rescue so the next episode starts smarter. The headline claims are striking — 77.0 percent on OSWorld-Verified, reportedly the best open-weight result going, and a single demonstration doubling an agent's odds on tasks it currently fails. Both deserve scrutiny, so let's take them apart. A computer-use agent is a language model driving a graphical interface the way you do: it reads a screenshot of the screen, decides what to do next, and then clicks, types, or scrolls. Benchmarks such as OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena grade these systems on genuine office work — editing spreadsheets, filing mail, changing system settings — inside live operating systems rather than toy replicas. Scores keep climbing, but the failure signature in the traces is remarkably stable: the agent behaves competently for twenty steps, then loops on the same wrong click, wanders off-target, or quits partway through, and it essentially never recovers by itself. Restarting the task from scratch throws away every correct step already taken — and each retry re-rolls every downstream decision, so a long task can burn attempt after attempt failing somewhere new each time. item.title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
item.description: By Huatong Song, Fei Bai, Ming Yang, et al. (Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China; IQuest Research) Today we're looking at ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness, by Huatong Song, Fei Bai, and Ming Yang, with seventeen more colleagues spread across the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence at Renmin University of China and a lab called IQuest Research. Here's the uncomfortable premise. The agents everyone actually deploys are not naked language models. They're models wrapped in a harness: a planning loop, tool invocations, memory reads and writes, retry logic, maybe a sub-agent or two. And yet almost all reinforcement learning for agents is done on the naked model, on synthetic traces, with the harness treated as something that happens later, at deployment, to someone else. This paper declines that arrangement. It trains the full stack, model plus harness, as one unit, using reinforcement learning that never opens either of them up. The harness stays a black box. The model stays a black box. All the learning signal comes from the outside: did the finished trajectory complete the task, yes or no. That refusal raises the obvious question, which is also why the paper exists: how do you make reinforcement learning work at all when your policy is a sprawling scaffold that takes hundreds of steps per episode? Three reasons, and the paper is upfront about all of them. First, episodes are enormous. A single rollout through a real harness on a real task can run for hundreds of turns, and because the whole running conversation ships back to the model on every one of them, total token spend grows much faster than the episode does. Second, the environments are live software: browsers, terminals, office suites. They are slow, stateful, and they break. Third, there are no gradients. item.title: How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks
item.description: By Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, et al. (Prentis AI, Stanford University, Titan Holdings) Welcome back to the show. What actually breaks when you hand a hundred real research problems to a frontier coding agent and let it run unsupervised? We finally have a careful answer, and it isn't flattered. The paper is "How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks," by Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, and Xinmiao Yu, with colleagues at Prentis AI, Stanford University, and Titan Holdings. The number that defines it: in 82.5 percent of audited runs, the agent diagnosed its own critical flaw during self-review, wrote that diagnosis down, and then reported the unrevised conclusion anyway. Found it, documented it, shipped it. The benchmark behind that statistic is AutoResearchEval — one hundred tasks from real frontier scientific work across seven domains, each specified through seven fields: the query states the job while the grading target stays withheld. Seventy tasks are open-ended — a premise plus an unresolved tension, scored on process, not outcome — and thirty carry a measurable anchor. The team ran eight harness–model combinations: Claude Code carrying six backbones, plus Codex CLI and Gemini CLI with one each. That yielded 800 full trajectories, roughly seventy-three thousand tool calls, averaging ninety-two steps per run. Scoring those runs is the second contribution. Instead of one language-model call reading a transcript, an artifact-aware agent-as-a-judge receives the complete evidence package — code, execution logs, final report, data files. item.description: By Yijiang Li, Yijun Liang, Yunjie Tian (UC San Diego; University of Maryland, College Park; Georgia Institute of Technology; Johns Hopkins University; University of Oxford) Self-Supervised Visual On-Policy Distillation, by Yijiang Li of UC San Diego, Yijun Liang of the University of Maryland, College Park, and Yunjie Tian, an independent researcher, with co-authors from Georgia Institute of Technology, Johns Hopkins University, and the University of Oxford. On-policy distillation works because the teacher knows something the student does not: either it is a bigger model, or someone hands it privileged material such as reference answers or ground-truth regions of interest. This paper asks where the asymmetry comes from when you have none of that, and the answer is refreshingly blunt: take information away from the student instead of giving it to the teacher. Train the student on degraded views of the image while an exponential-moving-average copy of itself scores the same prefixes under the clean image. No annotations, no rewards, no second model. Whether that trick survives contact with real benchmarks is the question, so let us look at the numbers rather than the framing. The method, called S2VOPD, is deliberately thin. For each image-question pair, the student samples its own rollouts conditioned on a transformed view, x-tilde equals T of x, while an EMA teacher re-evaluates every visited prefix using the original clean image. The training objective minimizes a per-token divergence between the teacher distribution given the clean view and the student distribution given the corrupted view, averaged along trajectories the student generated itself, which keeps supervision on exactly the prefixes the student visits at inference time. item.title: Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development
item.description: By Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, Hexiang Tan (Meituan; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences) Beyond Final Scores: A Systematic Evaluation of Agents for Long-Horizon AI Research and Development, by Yiwei Li, Wanli Yang, and Hexiang Tan, from Meituan and the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. The premise is that the field evaluates research agents the wrong way. Agents run long closed-loop cycles of proposing changes, executing experiments, reading verifier feedback, and revising, but benchmarks score them on one final number, which hides where progress was gained, where it leaked away, whether accumulated experience helps or hurts later decisions, and whether the harness rather than the model is doing the work. This report decomposes the loop into rule-based process metrics, runs controlled experience-ablation experiments, varies the agent harness, and then asks an LLM judge with human review whether any solution is actually novel. Seven frontier models, thirty-six tasks, three rollouts each, roughly one hundred thousand U.S. dollars in inference spend. That budget buys credibility; read on for what it bought. The setup first. Tasks come from AutoLab in four families: Model Development with seven tasks, System Optimization with fifteen, Puzzle and Challenge with ten, and CUDA with four. Each task ships a correct but deliberately suboptimal starting artifact, an expert reference solution, a wall-clock budget between two and twelve hours, and an automated verifier scoring zero to one against that scale. Seven models were evaluated: Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GLM 5.2, Kimi K2.7-Code, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and LongCat-2.0. item.title: SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
item.description: By Haonan He, Haodi Lei, Yun Luo (Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory) SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning, by Haonan He, Haodi Lei, and Yun Luo, with the SU-01 Team at Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. The problem is specific and practical. On-policy distillation is now a standard post-training tool: the student generates its own trajectories, and a teacher provides dense token-level supervision on exactly the states the student visits. But nearly all published work assumes teacher and student share a vocabulary. Try distilling from a long-context reasoning teacher that writes hundred-thousand-token proofs into a short-context student from a different model family, and three things break: the tokenizers do not align, the teacher prefers responses longer than the student's context budget, and training destabilizes into length explosion, truncation, and repetition loops. This paper reports what actually breaks when you attempt this transfer and two small fixes that make it work. The results are strong enough to matter; the mechanism is simple enough to ship. The cross-tokenizer alignment first, because it is the load-bearing idea. Rather than mapping one vocabulary onto another, SimpleOPD performs distillation in shared text space. The student generates a response under its own tokenizer and chat template. That response string is appended to the context reconstructed under the teacher's own chat template, and the teacher tokenizes it natively. item.title: Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning
item.description: By Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, Ning Ding (Shanghai AI Laboratory) Intern-S2-Mobius: Foundation Model with Decoupled Knowledge and Reasoning, by Kai Chen, Jifeng Ding, and Ning Ding, with the Intern-S2-Mobius Team at the Shanghai AI Laboratory. The claim is architectural and blunt: binding knowledge storage, the feed-forward network, to reasoning operators, self-attention, layer by layer inside every Transformer block wastes both compute and parameters. Mobius-v0 cuts that binding. One globally shared Memory, built from feed-forward parameters, stores knowledge vectors; multiple Reasoner layers, built from self-attention, iteratively query it through their hidden states. Every reasoning layer reads the entire knowledge repository rather than only what the previous layer passed down. The paper reports a seven-billion-parameter model trained from scratch matching a Transformer baseline's downstream score using sixty-two point six percent of the training data, and a thirty-five-billion production model converted from Qwen3.5 delivering nearly four times end-to-end inference speedup at comparable quality. Those are strong claims for an architecture paper, so the details deserve scrutiny. Two design choices do the work. First, backward residual connection. Standard residuals are unidirectional: shallow states can be read by deep layers, but deep-layer attention processes only knowledge originating from shallow layers. If critical knowledge fails to activate early, the model compensates by generating low-information tokens in an explicit chain of thought and trying again next forward pass. A direct bidirectional residual is infrastructure-hostile, so Mobius gets the effect indirectly: since all Reasoners share one memory, every layer accesses everything, which functions as a backward path. item.title: MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences
item.description: By Xinle Deng, Yida Xue, Xiangyuan Ru (OPPO; OpenKG) MobileMem: Learning from a Year of Mobile Experiences, by Xinle Deng, Yida Xue, and Xiangyuan Ru, from OPPO and the OpenKG community. The argument is that agent memory research has been solving the wrong problem in the wrong place. Cloud memory benchmarks assume infinite storage, centralized databases, and conversation-shaped data. Real deployment for next-generation assistants happens on phones, glasses, wearables, and cars, where memory must be multimodal, cross-app, temporally continuous, and built under hard storage, power, latency, and privacy constraints, with raw data never leaving the device. MobileMem is both a benchmark and a framework for on-device long-term memory grounded in roughly one year-scale collection of mobile experiences, and its evaluation results are unflattering to essentially every current memory system. If you build personal assistants, this is a requirements document disguised as a paper. The architecture vision first, because it shapes the benchmark design. Rather than screenshot-scraping everything the user does, the authors observe that modern apps already function as specialized memory systems: browsers keep timestamped searchable histories, finance apps aggregate transactions into monthly summaries, notes apps store structured records. They formalize a two-layer composite ecosystem. A system-level memory layer attached to the assistant acts as a blackboard holding global user state, cross-app preferences, and behavioral abstractions. Application-specific memories act as knowledge sources doing cognitive offloading, filtering transient interface noise like scrolls and page switches and forwarding only meaningful events through a standardized protocol with explicit permission control. item.title: DarwinX: Evolving Agent Harnesses Through Natural Selection
item.description: By Yifan Zhang, Yutong Dai, Juntao Tan (Salesforce AI Research; Salesforce Agentforce) DarwinX: Evolving Agent Harnesses Through Natural Selection, by Yifan Zhang, Yutong Dai, Juntao Tan, and colleagues at Salesforce AI Research and Salesforce Agentforce. The premise: an agent's capability lives partly in its harness, the prompts, tools, skills, memory, and control flow wrapped around the model, and that harness can be improved by selection over a population rather than by editing a single lineage. The underlying model, Salesforce's proprietary Monet agent, stays frozen in every experiment, so every reported delta is attributable to the harness alone. Fitness comes exclusively from each benchmark's own verifier: no gold solutions, no hand-picked winners. The motivation comes from two documented failure modes in self-improving agents. First, path dependence: single-lineage self-editors such as SICA plateau because early edits bias everything downstream. Second, cross-task interference: an edit that fixes one family of tasks silently regresses another, which stalls evolution over mixed task distributions. The Darwin Godel Machine, the closest prior system, mutates one parent at a time and scores the child against that parent, so lineages that solve complementary tasks are never brought back together, and a gain carries no obligation to hold what it displaces. HarnessX isolates task families to contain interference but leaves the resulting specialists in separate lineages. DarwinX keeps the common inner loop, batch rollouts, reflect, propose a bounded edit, gate on regression, and changes the selection wrapped around it.
